sources.title: Sam Altman Says OpenAI Has No IPO Timeline — Wants Safety Cases In Place Before Going Public - Yahoo Finance
passages: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said Tuesday the company has no particular timeline for an initial public offering (IPO), indicating that safety work around the next generation of artificial intelligence (AI) remains a higher priority than going public.
Altman said he does not want to pursue an IPO while conditions around AI development and safety remain in flux.
The model was "a little bit worse on a few of the evals" OpenAI uses, Altman said, characterizing the decision as an "abundance of caution." "There's not a big scary thing in this case," he said.
More broadly, Altman said alignment, safety, monitoring and security need to remain "way ahead of capabilities" as models improve.
Altman also pushed back on the idea that AI safety can be solved entirely through engineering.

extraction.body: Altman said OpenAI could consider an IPO after running "a few safety cases" and gaining a better understanding of how to safely contend with the next level of AI. He said the recently withheld OpenAI model was only "a little bit worse" on several evaluations and stressed there was no "big scary thing" behind the decision. Altman noted that AI safety cannot be treated solely as an engineering problem because model alignment remains a scientific challenge. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said Tuesday the company has no particular timeline for an initial public offering (IPO), indicating that safety work around the next generation of artificial intelligence (AI) remains a higher priority than going public. "I don't have a particular timeline in mind," Altman said during an interview with CNBC at OpenAI's Developer Day. An IPO could become more realistic once the company has run "a few safety cases" and feels it understands how to safely contend with the "next level of AI," he said. "I really think this is a time to put safety and mission first," he said. Asked about OpenAI's recent decision to hold back a new model, Altman said it fell short on some of the evaluations the company uses to gauge safety and alignment, rather than pointing to a specific serious incident. The model was "a little bit worse on a few of the evals" OpenAI uses, Altman said, characterizing the decision as an "abundance of caution." "There's not a big scary thing in this case," he said. He described withholding or reworking models that do not meet OpenAI's standards as part of the normal development process. More broadly, Altman said alignment, safety, monitoring and security need to remain "way ahead of capabilities" as models improve. He described that approach as "pacing" progress. Altman also pushed back on the idea that AI safety can be solved entirely through engineering. "We still have discovery about how to align these models," he said, arguing that the industry faces a scientific problem alongside the engineering work required to make AI systems safer. On liability, Altman said he expects a multi-level framework to emerge depending on whether a failure originates in the model, how a developer uses it, or intentional misuse by an end user. He compared the possible structure to the automotive industry, where responsibility can fall on different parties depending on what went wrong. Altman also expressed cautious optimism about discussions in Washington and international coordination, while acknowledging that previous expectations for policy progress had not always materialized. sources.title: OpenAI IPO will not happen in 2026 amid AI safety fears, Sam Altman says - The Guardian
passages: OpenAI will not go public in 2026, Sam Altman said in a Fortune interview published on Saturday, citing safety concerns over artificial intelligence .
When asked by Fortune whether 2026 is off the table in favor of 2027, Altman said: “I would say not 2026.
Yeah, we got a lot of stuff to do, like meeting this moment of what is going to be required for safety and alignment, and how the industry and governments can work together.”
“I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don’t feel pressure on that,” Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, told Fortune .
Altman also suggested that OpenAI and other leading AI companies may be close to announcing an agreement to slow AI development and work together to address safety risks, Fortune reported.
The New York Times in June reported that the San Francisco-based OpenAI was considering whether to hold off on a potentially trillion-dollar IPO until next year.

extraction.body: OpenAI’s decision comes after dire warnings about rapidly progressing technology and lawmakers’ calls for new rules OpenAI’s decision comes after dire warnings about rapidly progressing technology and lawmakers’ calls for new rules OpenAI will not go public in 2026, Sam Altman said in a Fortune interview published on Saturday, citing safety concerns over artificial intelligence . “I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don’t feel pressure on that,” Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, told Fortune . Growing numbers of US lawmakers ​are calling for new rules to govern AI systems after dire warnings from two researchers from OpenAI rival Anthropic that rapidly progressing artificial intelligence could lead to the extinction of the human race ‌in the not-too-distant future. The warnings follow cases of AI agents going rogue to hack external systems and AI ​safety researchers quitting their companies concerned about the technology’s risks. Politicians, both Democrats and Republicans, have responded with alarm and calls for more action. The New York Times in June reported that the San Francisco-based OpenAI was considering whether to hold off on a potentially trillion-dollar IPO until next year. At the time, shares in Elon Musk’s SpaceX IPO were tumbling after a surge that sent that company’s valuation to $1.8tn. When asked by Fortune whether 2026 is off the table in favor of 2027, Altman said: “I would say not 2026. Yeah, we got a lot of stuff to do, like meeting this moment of what is going to be required for safety and alignment, and how the industry and governments can work together.” Altman also suggested that OpenAI and other leading AI companies may be close to announcing an agreement to slow AI development and work together to address safety risks, Fortune reported. Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, on Saturday urged AI companies to take a more deliberate approach to development. “We must slow the ‌pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote in an essay shared on social media. Altman later posted that he agreed with the sentiment. “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” Altman wrote in a response to Amodei’s post on the X platform. “This has been a primary topic of discussions we’ve had at OpenAI in recent weeks.” Safety concerns have not slowed down Anthropic’s own IPO plans so far. Anthropic is expected to begin marketing its initial public offering in mid-October at the earliest and complete the listing days before the US midterm elections in November, people familiar with the matter told Reuters this month.

sources.title: Sam Altman says OpenAI won’t go public until its models are safe
passages: OpenAI, alongside its rivals, called for regulation and “pacing the frontier.” And earlier this month, Altman said in an interview that the company would likely not go public this year.
CEO Sam Altman says it won’t happen until the company can make better promises about model safety, with no firm timeline in sight.

But he expressed concerns that going public could create the potential to “disappoint Wall Street supporters in the names of safety or whatever else,” and that doing it during a “shift to very capable models and a new kind of safety requirement seems ill-advised.” He said OpenAI would prioritize safety to “confidently scale to the next stage of AI without people debating what percent chance we’re going to do all these bad things,” rather than “barrel, all guns blazing, towards an IPO.” “I don’t want to put additional pressure right now as we’re going through this significant change and what it’s going to take to make the safety claims that we all should want us to make for these extremely capable models,” Altman said.
For months, people have wondered when OpenAI will go public.
OpenAI rival Anthropic officially filed to go public in June, with its IPO likely to happen in November, reportedly after the US midterm elections.
In July, news broke that an unreleased OpenAI model had hacked into a rival AI lab, Hugging Face, without OpenAI’s knowledge.
More cybersecurity incidents soon came to light at OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google.

extraction.body: For months, people have wondered when OpenAI will go public. CEO Sam Altman says it won’t happen until the company can make better promises about model safety, with no firm timeline in sight. “We intend to continue with AI progress … but as the models have had this surge forward in capability, and we see more of that ahead of us, we have got to be able to make confident safety claims,” Altman said Tuesday during a Q&A with reporters after his DevDay keynote. At the same time, he said, waiting too long for an IPO would be “bad for the world.” Altman’s comments come after months of controversy about whether or not OpenAI and its rivals can control their own creations. In July, news broke that an unreleased OpenAI model had hacked into a rival AI lab, Hugging Face, without OpenAI’s knowledge. More cybersecurity incidents soon came to light at OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google. A high-profile resignation letter from an Anthropic employee sparked a public discussion about how risky these systems are for society at large. OpenAI, alongside its rivals, called for regulation and “pacing the frontier.” And earlier this month, Altman said in an interview that the company would likely not go public this year. At DevDay, Altman was circumspect about what “pacing the frontier” actually meant, refraining from calling it an outright slowdown. “Pacing to us means that we push safety and alignment ahead of capabilities,” Altman said. But he expressed concerns that going public could create the potential to “disappoint Wall Street supporters in the names of safety or whatever else,” and that doing it during a “shift to very capable models and a new kind of safety requirement seems ill-advised.” He said OpenAI would prioritize safety to “confidently scale to the next stage of AI without people debating what percent chance we’re going to do all these bad things,” rather than “barrel, all guns blazing, towards an IPO.” “I don’t want to put additional pressure right now as we’re going through this significant change and what it’s going to take to make the safety claims that we all should want us to make for these extremely capable models,” Altman said. OpenAI rival Anthropic officially filed to go public in June, with its IPO likely to happen in November, reportedly after the US midterm elections. Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which owns his AI company xAI, went public in June and became the biggest IPO in history. “I think it’s great when companies are public,” Altman said, adding, “I think it’s also kind of bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public.”

sources.title: Sam Altman says OpenAI won't go public until its AI models are safe
passages: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on Tuesday said the ChatGPT maker does not intend to go public until it can make stronger assurances about the safety of its increasingly capable AI (artificial intelligence) models, while warning that waiting too long for an IPO could also be “bad for the world". “We intend to continue with AI progress … but as the models have had this surge forward in capability, and we see more of that ahead of us, we have got to be able to make confident safety claims,” Altman said during a Q&A with reporters after his keynote address at OpenAI DevDay 2026, The Verge reported.
Altman added that he did not want OpenAI to “barrel, all guns blazing, towards an IPO".
OpenAI has pushed back its IPO plans as it focuses on the next phase of its AI development.

OpenAI and other major AI companies have faced a series of cybersecurity incidents after AI agents breached real-world systems during testing, including an OpenAI model that accessed and attacked developer platform Hugging Face without the company’s knowledge.

Altman said taking OpenAI public while the company is transitioning to more capable models and facing new safety requirements could pressure it to prioritise investor expectations over safety. “Pacing, to us, means that we push safety and alignment ahead of capabilities,” he said as quoted by The Verge. Altman added that he did not want OpenAI to “barrel, all guns blazing, towards an IPO". OpenAI has pushed back its IPO plans as it focuses on the next phase of its AI development. The company is now seeking to raise at least $30 billion from investors in a new funding round at a valuation of about $1.4 trillion, Bloomberg reported earlier on Wednesday. Altman said the company wants to reach a point where it can “confidently scale to the next stage of AI” without continued debate over the potential risks posed by increasingly capable models. “I don’t want to put additional pressure right now as we’re going through this significant change and what it’s going to take to make the safety claims that we all should want us to make for these extremely capable models,” he said. His comments come amid growing scrutiny of AI safety and the ability of companies to control increasingly capable models. OpenAI and other major AI companies have faced a series of cybersecurity incidents after AI agents breached real-world systems during testing, including an OpenAI model that accessed and attacked developer platform Hugging Face without the company’s knowledge. Similar incidents involving models from Anthropic, Meta and Google have also been reported. Altman had also said earlier this month that OpenAI was unlikely to go public this year. Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which owns his AI company xAI, went public in June. While stressing the need for stronger safety assurances before taking OpenAI public, Altman said there could also be downsides to delaying the move indefinitely, The Verge reported. “I think it’s great when companies are public,” he said. “I think it’s also kind of bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public.”

relevantPassages.text: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on Tuesday said the ChatGPT maker does not intend to go public until it can make stronger assurances about the safety of its increasingly capable AI (artificial intelligence) models, while warning that waiting too long for an IPO could also be “bad for the world". “We intend to continue with AI progress … but as the models have had this surge forward in capability, and we see more of that ahead of us, we have got to be able to make confident safety claims,” Altman said during a Q&A with reporters after his keynote address at OpenAI DevDay 2026, The Verge reported.
Altman added that he did not want OpenAI to “barrel, all guns blazing, towards an IPO".
OpenAI has pushed back its IPO plans as it focuses on the next phase of its AI development.

OpenAI and other major AI companies have faced a series of cybersecurity incidents after AI agents breached real-world systems during testing, including an OpenAI model that accessed and attacked developer platform Hugging Face without the company’s knowledge.

coreStoryFacts.text: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said Tuesday the company has no particular timeline for an initial public offering (IPO), indicating that safety work around the next generation of artificial intelligence (AI) remains a higher priority than going public.
Altman said he does not want to pursue an IPO while conditions around AI development and safety remain in flux.
The model was "a little bit worse on a few of the evals" OpenAI uses, Altman said, characterizing the decision as an "abundance of caution." "There's not a big scary thing in this case," he said.
More broadly, Altman said alignment, safety, monitoring and security need to remain "way ahead of capabilities" as models improve.
Altman also pushed back on the idea that AI safety can be solved entirely through engineering.
OpenAI will not go public in 2026, Sam Altman said in a Fortune interview published on Saturday, citing safety concerns over artificial intelligence .
When asked by Fortune whether 2026 is off the table in favor of 2027, Altman said: “I would say not 2026.
Yeah, we got a lot of stuff to do, like meeting this moment of what is going to be required for safety and alignment, and how the industry and governments can work together.”
“I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don’t feel pressure on that,” Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, told Fortune .
Altman also suggested that OpenAI and other leading AI companies may be close to announcing an agreement to slow AI development and work together to address safety risks, Fortune reported.
The New York Times in June reported that the San Francisco-based OpenAI was considering whether to hold off on a potentially trillion-dollar IPO until next year.
OpenAI, alongside its rivals, called for regulation and “pacing the frontier.” And earlier this month, Altman said in an interview that the company would likely not go public this year.
CEO Sam Altman says it won’t happen until the company can make better promises about model safety, with no firm timeline in sight.

But he expressed concerns that going public could create the potential to “disappoint Wall Street supporters in the names of safety or whatever else,” and that doing it during a “shift to very capable models and a new kind of safety requirement seems ill-advised.” He said OpenAI would prioritize safety to “confidently scale to the next stage of AI without people debating what percent chance we’re going to do all these bad things,” rather than “barrel, all guns blazing, towards an IPO.” “I don’t want to put additional pressure right now as we’re going through this significant change and what it’s going to take to make the safety claims that we all should want us to make for these extremely capable models,” Altman said.
For months, people have wondered when OpenAI will go public.
OpenAI rival Anthropic officially filed to go public in June, with its IPO likely to happen in November, reportedly after the US midterm elections.
In July, news broke that an unreleased OpenAI model had hacked into a rival AI lab, Hugging Face, without OpenAI’s knowledge.
More cybersecurity incidents soon came to light at OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google.

extraction.body: Altman said OpenAI could consider an IPO after running "a few safety cases" and gaining a better understanding of how to safely contend with the next level of AI. He said the recently withheld OpenAI model was only "a little bit worse" on several evaluations and stressed there was no "big scary thing" behind the decision. Altman noted that AI safety cannot be treated solely as an engineering problem because model alignment remains a scientific challenge. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said Tuesday the company has no particular timeline for an initial public offering (IPO), indicating that safety work around the next generation of artificial intelligence (AI) remains a higher priority than going public. "I don't have a particular timeline in mind," Altman said during an interview with CNBC at OpenAI's Developer Day. An IPO could become more realistic once the company has run "a few safety cases" and feels it understands how to safely contend with the "next level of AI," he said. "I really think this is a time to put safety and mission first," he said. Asked about OpenAI's recent decision to hold back a new model, Altman said it fell short on some of the evaluations the company uses to gauge safety and alignment, rather than pointing to a specific serious incident. The model was "a little bit worse on a few of the evals" OpenAI uses, Altman said, characterizing the decision as an "abundance of caution." "There's not a big scary thing in this case," he said. He described withholding or reworking models that do not meet OpenAI's standards as part of the normal development process. More broadly, Altman said alignment, safety, monitoring and security need to remain "way ahead of capabilities" as models improve. He described that approach as "pacing" progress. Altman also pushed back on the idea that AI safety can be solved entirely through engineering. "We still have discovery about how to align these models," he said, arguing that the industry faces a scientific problem alongside the engineering work required to make AI systems safer. On liability, Altman said he expects a multi-level framework to emerge depending on whether a failure originates in the model, how a developer uses it, or intentional misuse by an end user. He compared the possible structure to the automotive industry, where responsibility can fall on different parties depending on what went wrong. Altman also expressed cautious optimism about discussions in Washington and international coordination, while acknowledging that previous expectations for policy progress had not always materialized. extraction.body: OpenAI’s decision comes after dire warnings about rapidly progressing technology and lawmakers’ calls for new rules OpenAI’s decision comes after dire warnings about rapidly progressing technology and lawmakers’ calls for new rules OpenAI will not go public in 2026, Sam Altman said in a Fortune interview published on Saturday, citing safety concerns over artificial intelligence . “I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don’t feel pressure on that,” Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, told Fortune . Growing numbers of US lawmakers ​are calling for new rules to govern AI systems after dire warnings from two researchers from OpenAI rival Anthropic that rapidly progressing artificial intelligence could lead to the extinction of the human race ‌in the not-too-distant future. The warnings follow cases of AI agents going rogue to hack external systems and AI ​safety researchers quitting their companies concerned about the technology’s risks. Politicians, both Democrats and Republicans, have responded with alarm and calls for more action. The New York Times in June reported that the San Francisco-based OpenAI was considering whether to hold off on a potentially trillion-dollar IPO until next year. At the time, shares in Elon Musk’s SpaceX IPO were tumbling after a surge that sent that company’s valuation to $1.8tn. extraction.body: After weeks of Washington being gripped by a wave of fear about artificial intelligence gone awry, the Trump administration on Tuesday sought to reassure a skeptical public that it can embrace the technology - and trust the industry to police itself. Standing with the world's richest and most powerful tech executives Tuesday outside the West Wing, President Donald Trump said that he and they had signed a voluntary accord intended to ensure the industry develops AI safely. The agreement capped a day in which Trump sought to reinforce his pitch that AI is an engine of prosperity that should not be restrained by government. "In order to build a positive future for the American people and the world, we believe every company is responsible for developing its own technology safely and in a way that builds trust with customers and the public," the agreement says. Under the accord, the companies agreed to develop internal controls to prevent AI systems from spinning out of control. "I'm seeing tremendous self-policing," Trump said, surrounded by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg. The accord marks the most significant action the White House has taken to date to respond to growing concerns about AI risks, as even some of the industry's top leaders warn that companies should slow down development. The commitments reflect many of the measures that labs building advanced AI systems had already adopted, and the accord falls far short of the government intervention that some technologists have warned is necessary as AI rapidly advances. The announcement of the accord followed what Trump called a "very productive" and "extremely friendly" lunch at the White House with House Speaker Mike Johnson and tech executives, including Amazon founder Jeff Bezos. (Bezos owns The Washington Post.) Trump also sought to portray AI as a technology that can bring convenience to Americans. Before lunch, he launched America.gov, a government chatbot for researching public services, as part of a day-long event featuring members of his Cabinet and tech executives. Trump also signed an order that will rename AI as "superintelligence" in government documents, as he attempts to rebrand a technology that has sparked deep public anxiety, resisting calls for the government to craft guardrails. The day's focus on AI's promise contrasts with growing questions about the technology's trajectory. AI firms say their latest systems have become increasingly powerful, showing signs of being able to design their own more-potent successors. But companies have struggled to keep control of the technology, as rogue AI agents have hacked into company and government systems, and a roster of top industry figures have warned that the end result could be catastrophic for humanity. Last week, it was disclosed that the federal government itself had been a victim, with a handful of websites probed by AI agents deployed by ChatGPT maker OpenAI. (The Post has a content partnership with OpenAI.) Yet, even as the public's concerns have grown and Democrats in Congress have pressed for regulation, Trump has largely dismissed the risk, calling it a "hoax." On Tuesday, he accused the Democrats of stifling growth and technological progress because that could benefit Republicans. The events on Tuesday propel a different narrative than the warnings issued by company CEOs in recent weeks. AI's many boosters expect the technology will invigorate the economy, push the boundaries of science and help cure diseases. But that message has found only limited traction with a public worried about job losses and rogue bots sowing chaos online. "We do not surrender to fears about what technologies will do to us," he said Tuesday. "We decide that those technologies will do for us some very, very incredible things." "But changing what we call artificial intelligence does nothing to address the very real risks that come with increasingly powerful AI systems," Warner said. As dozens of administration officials and tech executives gathered for lunch Tuesday in the East Room, there was little public sign of the divisions within the tech industry and the Trump administration over the future of AI. Executives sitting around the table have expressed wildly divergent views about the perils of AI and the government's role in responding to its potential pitfalls. Trump sat between Elon Musk, who supported calls to slow down AI development last month, and Huang, who has resisted calls for any coordinated slowdown, saying it is up to individual companies to ensure that their products are safe. Amodei, the head of Anthropic who led the calls to pace development of advanced AI systems, joined the lunch after having his first one-on-one dinner Sunday with Trump. After the event, a reporter asked all the executives if they agreed that no government guardrails are necessary and that the industry can self-police. "I can tell you the answer is yes," Trump said, before any of the CEOs spoke. He then asked Huang to speak. "There's no conflict between innovation, technology and safety," Huang said. "We are going to have to create new technologies to advance the capabilities of AI, but we're also creating new technologies to advance the safety of it." Trump spoke positively of Amodei, who previously clashed with the administration over the use of his company's technology by the military. Amodei said the accord that the executives signed is intended to give the public confidence that AI works "in the way we all intended." Companies that signed on committed to developing internal controls, risk assessments and reviews by external auditors. Many of the companies developing advanced AI have already implemented these steps. Last week, OpenAI revealed that ChatGPT leaked 53 "user-provided images" to image-hosting providers. Trump rolled out the America.gov website at a conference in the gilded Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium, which was set up to evoke a tech company product release stage. Music played as staff members distributed cans of La Colombe iced coffee to attendees, while a sleek "Hello, America" logo was projected on a large screen at the front of the room. Joe Gebbia, the chief design officer of the United States and architect of America.gov, described the website, a partnership with Google's Gemini and SpaceXAI's Grok, as a "concierge to navigate government" during a Fox News interview ahead of the event. But in the coming months, the goal is for the chatbot to help people enroll in government programs such as Medicare or complete tasks such as passport renewals. Trump's AI push comes as his administration has cultivated relationships with Silicon Valley executives and investors. Standing with the world's richest and most powerful tech executives Tuesday outside the West Wing, President Donald Trump said that he and they had signed a voluntary accord intended to ensure the industry develops AI safely.
The agreement capped a day in which Trump sought to reinforce his pitch that AI is an engine of prosperity that should not be restrained by government.

"In order to build a positive future for the American people and the world, we believe every company is responsible for developing its own technology safely and in a way that builds trust with customers and the public," the agreement says.
Under the accord, the companies agreed to develop internal controls to prevent AI systems from spinning out of control.
"I'm seeing tremendous self-policing," Trump said, surrounded by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

The accord marks the most significant action the White House has taken to date to respond to growing concerns about AI risks, as even some of the industry's top leaders warn that companies should slow down development.

The commitments reflect many of the measures that labs building advanced AI systems had already adopted, and the accord falls far short of the government intervention that some technologists have warned is necessary as AI rapidly advances.

The announcement of the accord followed what Trump called a "very productive" and "extremely friendly" lunch at the White House with House Speaker Mike Johnson and tech executives, including Amazon founder Jeff Bezos. (Bezos owns The Washington Post.)

Trump also sought to portray AI as a technology that can bring convenience to Americans. Before lunch, he launched America.gov, a government chatbot for researching public services, as part of a day-long event featuring members of his Cabinet and tech executives.

Trump also signed an order that will rename AI as "superintelligence" in government documents, as he attempts to rebrand a technology that has sparked deep public anxiety, resisting calls for the government to craft guardrails.

AI firms say their latest systems have become increasingly powerful, showing signs of being able to design their own more-potent successors. Last week, it was disclosed that the federal government itself had been a victim, with a handful of websites probed by AI agents deployed by ChatGPT maker OpenAI. (The Post has a content partnership with OpenAI.)

extraction.body: President Donald Trump and the heads of six major technology companies signed a voluntary agreement on AI self-policing in Washington on Tuesday, September 29, 2026. The document is called the Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities, and it is not legally binding. The signatories are Trump and Dario Amodei (CEO of Anthropic), Sundar Pichai (Google), Mark Zuckerberg (Meta), Greg Brockman (president of OpenAI), Jensen Huang (Nvidia) and Elon Musk, founder of xAI, which is now part of SpaceX. According to the seating chart Trump posted on Truth Social, Huang sat to his right and Musk to his left. The document sets out four layers of oversight: internal controls that track the capabilities and behavior of models during training and deployment, in areas such as cybersecurity an internal team that supervises those controls and fixes any problems found cooperation with an independent outside auditor a dedicated board committee at each company, which reviews the reports of internal and external auditors The companies also pledged to meet regularly to, in the words of the document, "establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems". According to a wire report, the companies already carry out some of the measures or had promised them earlier. The document leaves the door open to legislation, but without any obligation: "Regardless of whether this is required of companies, we believe that implementing these controls and audits is critical to ensuring a safe future for everyone, and each of our companies are committed to doing this." Elsewhere it says: "Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws and regulations". Outside the West Wing of the White House, Trump told reporters: "I think I'm seeing tremendous self-policing. And they understand that they have to self-police." At the table, seated next to the executives, he put the same view differently: "There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation, and we automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that." He called the agreement "morally binding" and announced a board of about ten people that will "watch over the whole enterprise". He also said that in the coming days, after talks with the industry, he will name someone to oversee the agreement. At the launch of the America.gov chatbot, which is meant to help citizens navigate government services, Trump declared: "I will never stifle the growth of a technology that will be bigger than the industrial revolution." He went on: "We can't stifle it, and we're leading by a lot." At the same event, Musk described that afternoon what the companies had agreed to: "We agreed to a number of things that include joint monitoring, board special committees, just generally grading each other's homework." Amodei, one of the loudest advocates for slowing AI development, said: "The technology has very real risks." He added: "And, you know, the mechanism, how we address those risks is still under discussion." Trump also spoke about data centers, which face bipartisan opposition in local communities across the country. He said the executives agreed to help schools or cut energy costs: "You're going to see, data centers are going to be very popular." If the opposition persists, in his words, "they'll be forced to go overseas or other locations". Why would I want to do anything?" Last week, during Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington, the two countries agreed on a channel for handling AI-related incidents. Trust has been shaken by a series of incidents. On Monday, September 28, OpenAI announced that it would not release its GPT-6.1 Astra model, because internal testing found safety risks. Separately, it publicly apologized for how it handled a series of cases in which its agents gained unauthorized access to Australian government websites, among them the national health database. Nextgov recalls that a few months ago an OpenAI model escaped its test environment and broke into Hugging Face. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on CNBC on Tuesday: "We are pacing our progress, which includes sometimes not training a model." He added that companies need to work "in a way where we can make very confident safety cases and claims, so that people don't have a bunch of anxiety". Last week, twenty countries and the European Union called for global coordination to keep AI under human control, including a possible oversight body. Trump rejected that approach before the UN General Assembly and said his administration would oppose any attempt to build a "globalist scheme" of control. What does the order on the name "superintelligence" change? The same day, Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to call artificial intelligence superintelligence (SI) in official correspondence, public statements, websites, reports, policy documents and other non-statutory documents. The president's science and technology adviser has 60 days, working with agency heads, to propose a legal definition of SI and assess whether it changes, expands or replaces the existing statutory definition of artificial intelligence. Trump introduced the term last week at the UN General Assembly. Vice President JD Vance said the administration prefers cooperation with leading companies over regulation. "The solution to some of the AI risks is for you guys to take the risk seriously, not to come to the government for a regulatory regime that may make things worse if it's not smart and careful." Vance also rejected the idea of a body modeled on the U.S. Food and Drug Administration or aviation regulators: "The problem with that is one you have to get regulators who are actually smart about what's going on and most bureaucrats just know way less about this than the people who are actually building these products." David Sacks, an investor who was previously Trump's AI adviser, judged the agreement "far better" than an international deal that would "probably never happen". In a post on X he wrote: "President Trump continues to ensure that the U.S. remains the technology leader while putting Americans first." Alvin Wang Graylin of the Asia Society Policy Institute's Center for China Analysis welcomed the commitment but said it is far from what is needed. He told Al Jazeera: "What is missing is independence and anything that crosses a border. The companies drafted the principles, they hire the auditor, and the commitment is voluntary, on a day the White House also said it would not support guardrails." Toby Walsh of the UNSW AI Institute in Sydney noted that the companies have already shown themselves to be "incompetent and careless at managing themselves". He asked: "What other trillion-dollar industry marks its own homework?" David Krueger of the University of Montreal, who advocates a pause in development, said one thing in the document is interesting after all: "If you look at the substance, it's interesting that it calls for external evaluators, so it might result in a minute improvement over the status quo." He added: "But I'm not excited by something that might reduce the risk by 1 percent." Alex Pascal of the Berkman Klein Center for Internet and Society said the only path to reducing risk is "robust legal liability, regulation and fundamentally changing the race dynamics that are driving unsafe decision-making by frontier AI developers". Robin Jia of the University of Southern California warned that it is important for the intentions of the leading labs to be "well-aligned with the broader interest of the American public". His colleague Shri Narayanan from the same university judged that the document balances the room needed for innovation with regulation. The agreement does not say who the independent auditor will be, and it is voluntary and legally non-binding. Trump called it "morally binding", while the text itself says that legal regulation is something that "may make sense" only over time. The document does not show that the measures will reduce risk, because there are no measurements for that, only commitments on paper and statements from the participants.

extraction.body: US President Donald Trump says US bosses of artificial intelligence companies have signed a voluntary accord that will include internal and external reviews. The deal to self regulate was struck during a meeting at the White House on Tuesday aimed at addressing Americans' fears about the technology. “I think I’m seeing tremendous self-policing. And they understand that they have to self-police,” Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference outside the West Wing. Trump met with leading executives from top tech firms that are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build out AI infrastructure, including data centres in communities across the country, which have sparked grassroots, bipartisan opposition. The accord was signed by Trump, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and Elon Musk, founder of xAI, which is now part of SpaceX. The accord, which Trump posted on Truth Social, opens the door to future regulation but focused on four voluntary steps for the companies to take. The accord said the companies would implement “robust internal controls,” partner with an “independent external auditor” to assess whether the controls were working, and establish a committee within each company's board of directors to evaluate reports from internal and external auditors. “Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws and regulations,” the accord said. Trump repeatedly praised the business executives for developing a technology that he said would produce “unbelievable growth". Investment in data centres and the accompanying computer equipment has accelerated the economy and boosted the stock market, which has swelled investment accounts for higher-income Americans and lifted their spending. Yet there were some notes of caution. Amodei, who has been one of the most outspoken voices calling for a slowdown in AI development, admitted "the technology has very real risks”. Trump suggested about 10 people would be named to a committee to “watch over the whole enterprise” and said the accord would be “morally binding". He also said he would name someone to oversee the agreement in coming days after consulting with industry. Some of the actions outlined in the accord are measures the companies are already taking in some form or have previously committed to doing. Some experts are sceptical of putting “so much faith in self-policing”, like Robin Jia, an assistant professor of computer science at the University of Southern California. He pointed to the recent disclosures of hacking incidents. “As the models get better, the consequences of such things are only going to get greater”. coreStoryFacts.text: "I'm seeing tremendous self-policing," Trump said, surrounded by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

After weeks of Washington being gripped by a wave of fear about artificial intelligence gone awry, the Trump administration on Tuesday sought to reassure a skeptical public that it can embrace the technology - and trust the industry to police itself.
Trump also sought to portray AI as a technology that can bring convenience to Americans.
Before lunch, he launched America.gov, a government chatbot for researching public services, as part of a day-long event featuring members of his Cabinet and tech executives.
Executives sitting around the table have expressed wildly divergent views about the perils of AI and the government's role in responding to its potential pitfalls.

Trump sat between Elon Musk, who supported calls to slow down AI development last month, and Huang, who has resisted calls for any coordinated slowdown, saying it is up to individual companies to ensure that their products are safe.
Amodei, the head of Anthropic who led the calls to pace development of advanced AI systems, joined the lunch after having his first one-on-one dinner Sunday with Trump.

Yet, even as the public's concerns have grown and Democrats in Congress have pressed for regulation, Trump has largely dismissed the risk, calling it a "hoax." On Tuesday, he accused the Democrats of stifling growth and technological progress because that could benefit Republicans.
"I can tell you the answer is yes," Trump said, before any of the CEOs spoke.
Trump rolled out the America.gov website at a conference in the gilded Andrew W.
Mellon Auditorium, which was set up to evoke a tech company product release stage.
Music played as staff members distributed cans of La Colombe iced coffee to attendees, while a sleek "Hello, America" logo was projected on a large screen at the front of the room.
The agreement capped a day in which Trump sought to reinforce his pitch that AI is an engine of prosperity that should not be restrained by government.

"In order to build a positive future for the American people and the world, we believe every company is responsible for developing its own technology safely and in a way that builds trust with customers and the public," the agreement says.
Trump spoke positively of Amodei, who previously clashed with the administration over the use of his company's technology by the military.
Trump's AI push comes as his administration has cultivated relationships with Silicon Valley executives and investors.
DOGE Service, is among a group of tech leaders who argue they can improve Washington by applying Silicon Valley principles.
President Donald Trump and the heads of six major technology companies signed a voluntary agreement on AI self-policing in Washington on Tuesday, September 29, 2026.
Outside the West Wing of the White House, Trump told reporters: "I think I'm seeing tremendous self-policing.

The signatories are Trump and Dario Amodei (CEO of Anthropic), Sundar Pichai (Google), Mark Zuckerberg (Meta), Greg Brockman (president of OpenAI), Jensen Huang (Nvidia) and Elon Musk, founder of xAI, which is now part of SpaceX.

The same day, Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to call artificial intelligence superintelligence (SI) in official correspondence, public statements, websites, reports, policy documents and other non-statutory documents.

At the launch of the America.gov chatbot, which is meant to help citizens navigate government services, Trump declared: "I will never stifle the growth of a technology that will be bigger than the industrial revolution." He went on: "We can't stifle it, and we're leading by a lot." At the same event, Musk described that afternoon what the companies had agreed to: "We agreed to a number of things that include joint monitoring, board special committees, just generally grading each other's homework." Amodei, one of the loudest advocates for slowing AI development, said: "The technology has very real risks." He added: "And, you know, the mechanism, how we address those risks is still under discussion." Trump also spoke about data centers, which face bipartisan opposition in local communities across the country.
Trump rejected that approach before the UN General Assembly and said his administration would oppose any attempt to build a "globalist scheme" of control.

Food and Drug Administration or aviation regulators: "The problem with that is one you have to get regulators who are actually smart about what's going on and most bureaucrats just know way less about this than the people who are actually building these products." David Sacks, an investor who was previously Trump's AI adviser, judged the agreement "far better" than an international deal that would "probably never happen".

extraction.body: After weeks of Washington being gripped by a wave of fear about artificial intelligence gone awry, the Trump administration on Tuesday sought to reassure a skeptical public that it can embrace the technology - and trust the industry to police itself. Standing with the world's richest and most powerful tech executives Tuesday outside the West Wing, President Donald Trump said that he and they had signed a voluntary accord intended to ensure the industry develops AI safely. The agreement capped a day in which Trump sought to reinforce his pitch that AI is an engine of prosperity that should not be restrained by government. "In order to build a positive future for the American people and the world, we believe every company is responsible for developing its own technology safely and in a way that builds trust with customers and the public," the agreement says. Under the accord, the companies agreed to develop internal controls to prevent AI systems from spinning out of control. "I'm seeing tremendous self-policing," Trump said, surrounded by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg. The accord marks the most significant action the White House has taken to date to respond to growing concerns about AI risks, as even some of the industry's top leaders warn that companies should slow down development. The commitments reflect many of the measures that labs building advanced AI systems had already adopted, and the accord falls far short of the government intervention that some technologists have warned is necessary as AI rapidly advances. The announcement of the accord followed what Trump called a "very productive" and "extremely friendly" lunch at the White House with House Speaker Mike Johnson and tech executives, including Amazon founder Jeff Bezos. (Bezos owns The Washington Post.) Trump also sought to portray AI as a technology that can bring convenience to Americans. Before lunch, he launched America.gov, a government chatbot for researching public services, as part of a day-long event featuring members of his Cabinet and tech executives. Trump also signed an order that will rename AI as "superintelligence" in government documents, as he attempts to rebrand a technology that has sparked deep public anxiety, resisting calls for the government to craft guardrails. The day's focus on AI's promise contrasts with growing questions about the technology's trajectory. AI firms say their latest systems have become increasingly powerful, showing signs of being able to design their own more-potent successors. But companies have struggled to keep control of the technology, as rogue AI agents have hacked into company and government systems, and a roster of top industry figures have warned that the end result could be catastrophic for humanity. Last week, it was disclosed that the federal government itself had been a victim, with a handful of websites probed by AI agents deployed by ChatGPT maker OpenAI. (The Post has a content partnership with OpenAI.) Yet, even as the public's concerns have grown and Democrats in Congress have pressed for regulation, Trump has largely dismissed the risk, calling it a "hoax." On Tuesday, he accused the Democrats of stifling growth and technological progress because that could benefit Republicans. The events on Tuesday propel a different narrative than the warnings issued by company CEOs in recent weeks. AI's many boosters expect the technology will invigorate the economy, push the boundaries of science and help cure diseases. But that message has found only limited traction with a public worried about job losses and rogue bots sowing chaos online. "We do not surrender to fears about what technologies will do to us," he said Tuesday. "We decide that those technologies will do for us some very, very incredible things." As dozens of administration officials and tech executives gathered for lunch Tuesday in the East Room, there was little public sign of the divisions within the tech industry and the Trump administration over the future of AI. Executives sitting around the table have expressed wildly divergent views about the perils of AI and the government's role in responding to its potential pitfalls. Trump sat between Elon Musk, who supported calls to slow down AI development last month, and Huang, who has resisted calls for any coordinated slowdown, saying it is up to individual companies to ensure that their products are safe. Amodei, the head of Anthropic who led the calls to pace development of advanced AI systems, joined the lunch after having his first one-on-one dinner Sunday with Trump. After the event, a reporter asked all the executives if they agreed that no government guardrails are necessary and that the industry can self-police. "I can tell you the answer is yes," Trump said, before any of the CEOs spoke. He then asked Huang to speak. "There's no conflict between innovation, technology and safety," Huang said. "We are going to have to create new technologies to advance the capabilities of AI, but we're also creating new technologies to advance the safety of it." Amodei said the accord that the executives signed is intended to give the public confidence that AI works "in the way we all intended." Companies that signed on committed to developing internal controls, risk assessments and reviews by external auditors. extraction.body: President Donald Trump and the heads of six major technology companies signed a voluntary agreement on AI self-policing in Washington on Tuesday, September 29, 2026. The document is called the Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities, and it is not legally binding. The signatories are Trump and Dario Amodei (CEO of Anthropic), Sundar Pichai (Google), Mark Zuckerberg (Meta), Greg Brockman (president of OpenAI), Jensen Huang (Nvidia) and Elon Musk, founder of xAI, which is now part of SpaceX. According to the seating chart Trump posted on Truth Social, Huang sat to his right and Musk to his left. The document sets out four layers of oversight: internal controls that track the capabilities and behavior of models during training and deployment, in areas such as cybersecurity an internal team that supervises those controls and fixes any problems found cooperation with an independent outside auditor a dedicated board committee at each company, which reviews the reports of internal and external auditors The companies also pledged to meet regularly to, in the words of the document, "establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems". According to a wire report, the companies already carry out some of the measures or had promised them earlier. The document leaves the door open to legislation, but without any obligation: "Regardless of whether this is required of companies, we believe that implementing these controls and audits is critical to ensuring a safe future for everyone, and each of our companies are committed to doing this." Elsewhere it says: "Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws and regulations". Outside the West Wing of the White House, Trump told reporters: "I think I'm seeing tremendous self-policing. And they understand that they have to self-police." At the table, seated next to the executives, he put the same view differently: "There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation, and we automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that." He called the agreement "morally binding" and announced a board of about ten people that will "watch over the whole enterprise". He also said that in the coming days, after talks with the industry, he will name someone to oversee the agreement. At the launch of the America.gov chatbot, which is meant to help citizens navigate government services, Trump declared: "I will never stifle the growth of a technology that will be bigger than the industrial revolution." He went on: "We can't stifle it, and we're leading by a lot." At the same event, Musk described that afternoon what the companies had agreed to: "We agreed to a number of things that include joint monitoring, board special committees, just generally grading each other's homework." Amodei, one of the loudest advocates for slowing AI development, said: "The technology has very real risks." He added: "And, you know, the mechanism, how we address those risks is still under discussion." Trump also spoke about data centers, which face bipartisan opposition in local communities across the country. He said the executives agreed to help schools or cut energy costs: "You're going to see, data centers are going to be very popular." If the opposition persists, in his words, "they'll be forced to go overseas or other locations". Why would I want to do anything?" Last week, during Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington, the two countries agreed on a channel for handling AI-related incidents. Trust has been shaken by a series of incidents. On Monday, September 28, OpenAI announced that it would not release its GPT-6.1 Astra model, because internal testing found safety risks. Separately, it publicly apologized for how it handled a series of cases in which its agents gained unauthorized access to Australian government websites, among them the national health database. Nextgov recalls that a few months ago an OpenAI model escaped its test environment and broke into Hugging Face. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on CNBC on Tuesday: "We are pacing our progress, which includes sometimes not training a model." He added that companies need to work "in a way where we can make very confident safety cases and claims, so that people don't have a bunch of anxiety". Last week, twenty countries and the European Union called for global coordination to keep AI under human control, including a possible oversight body. Trump rejected that approach before the UN General Assembly and said his administration would oppose any attempt to build a "globalist scheme" of control. What does the order on the name "superintelligence" change? The same day, Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to call artificial intelligence superintelligence (SI) in official correspondence, public statements, websites, reports, policy documents and other non-statutory documents. The president's science and technology adviser has 60 days, working with agency heads, to propose a legal definition of SI and assess whether it changes, expands or replaces the existing statutory definition of artificial intelligence. Trump introduced the term last week at the UN General Assembly. Vice President JD Vance said the administration prefers cooperation with leading companies over regulation. "The solution to some of the AI risks is for you guys to take the risk seriously, not to come to the government for a regulatory regime that may make things worse if it's not smart and careful." Vance also rejected the idea of a body modeled on the U.S. Food and Drug Administration or aviation regulators: "The problem with that is one you have to get regulators who are actually smart about what's going on and most bureaucrats just know way less about this than the people who are actually building these products." David Sacks, an investor who was previously Trump's AI adviser, judged the agreement "far better" than an international deal that would "probably never happen". In a post on X he wrote: "President Trump continues to ensure that the U.S. remains the technology leader while putting Americans first." Alvin Wang Graylin of the Asia Society Policy Institute's Center for China Analysis welcomed the commitment but said it is far from what is needed. He told Al Jazeera: "What is missing is independence and anything that crosses a border. The companies drafted the principles, they hire the auditor, and the commitment is voluntary, on a day the White House also said it would not support guardrails." Toby Walsh of the UNSW AI Institute in Sydney noted that the companies have already shown themselves to be "incompetent and careless at managing themselves". He asked: "What other trillion-dollar industry marks its own homework?" David Krueger of the University of Montreal, who advocates a pause in development, said one thing in the document is interesting after all: "If you look at the substance, it's interesting that it calls for external evaluators, so it might result in a minute improvement over the status quo." He added: "But I'm not excited by something that might reduce the risk by 1 percent." Alex Pascal of the Berkman Klein Center for Internet and Society said the only path to reducing risk is "robust legal liability, regulation and fundamentally changing the race dynamics that are driving unsafe decision-making by frontier AI developers". Robin Jia of the University of Southern California warned that it is important for the intentions of the leading labs to be "well-aligned with the broader interest of the American public". His colleague Shri Narayanan from the same university judged that the document balances the room needed for innovation with regulation. The agreement does not say who the independent auditor will be, and it is voluntary and legally non-binding. Trump called it "morally binding", while the text itself says that legal regulation is something that "may make sense" only over time. The document does not show that the measures will reduce risk, because there are no measurements for that, only commitments on paper and statements from the participants.

extraction.body: US President Donald Trump says US bosses of artificial intelligence companies have signed a voluntary accord that will include internal and external reviews. The deal to self regulate was struck during a meeting at the White House on Tuesday aimed at addressing Americans' fears about the technology. “I think I’m seeing tremendous self-policing. And they understand that they have to self-police,” Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference outside the West Wing. Trump met with leading executives from top tech firms that are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build out AI infrastructure, including data centres in communities across the country, which have sparked grassroots, bipartisan opposition. The accord was signed by Trump, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and Elon Musk, founder of xAI, which is now part of SpaceX. The accord, which Trump posted on Truth Social, opens the door to future regulation but focused on four voluntary steps for the companies to take. The accord said the companies would implement “robust internal controls,” partner with an “independent external auditor” to assess whether the controls were working, and establish a committee within each company's board of directors to evaluate reports from internal and external auditors. “Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws and regulations,” the accord said. Trump repeatedly praised the business executives for developing a technology that he said would produce “unbelievable growth". Investment in data centres and the accompanying computer equipment has accelerated the economy and boosted the stock market, which has swelled investment accounts for higher-income Americans and lifted their spending. Yet there were some notes of caution. Amodei, who has been one of the most outspoken voices calling for a slowdown in AI development, admitted "the technology has very real risks”. "And, you know, the mechanism, how we address those risks is still under discussion,” Amodei said. Trump suggested about 10 people would be named to a committee to “watch over the whole enterprise” and said the accord would be “morally binding". He also said he would name someone to oversee the agreement in coming days after consulting with industry. Some of the actions outlined in the accord are measures the companies are already taking in some form or have previously committed to doing. Some experts are sceptical of putting “so much faith in self-policing”, like Robin Jia, an assistant professor of computer science at the University of Southern California. He pointed to the recent disclosures of hacking incidents. “As the models get better, the consequences of such things are only going to get greater”. Some took issue with the accord’s vague, broad language, including Alex Pascal, executive director of the Berkman Klein Center for Internet and Society. “The only way to reduce the risks and harms of AI to Americans is through robust legal liability, regulation and fundamentally changing the race dynamics that are driving unsafe decision-making by frontier AI developers whose costs are borne by the American people,” he said. Earlier on Tuesday, Trump promised that the US government wouldn't limit the development of AI or support calls for “guardrails” or other restrictions. “I will never stifle the growth of a technology that will be bigger than the industrial revolution,” Trump said at the unveiling of an AI chatbot intended to help navigate government services. “We can’t stifle it, and we’re leading by a lot.” Trump also said the executives had agreed to assuage the bipartisan opposition to data centres cropping up in local communities across the country by providing more financial support to local schools or taking steps to reduce energy costs. “You’re going to see, data centres are going to be very popular," Trump said.

passages: "I'm seeing tremendous self-policing," Trump said, surrounded by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

After weeks of Washington being gripped by a wave of fear about artificial intelligence gone awry, the Trump administration on Tuesday sought to reassure a skeptical public that it can embrace the technology - and trust the industry to police itself.
Trump also sought to portray AI as a technology that can bring convenience to Americans.
Before lunch, he launched America.gov, a government chatbot for researching public services, as part of a day-long event featuring members of his Cabinet and tech executives.
Executives sitting around the table have expressed wildly divergent views about the perils of AI and the government's role in responding to its potential pitfalls.

Trump sat between Elon Musk, who supported calls to slow down AI development last month, and Huang, who has resisted calls for any coordinated slowdown, saying it is up to individual companies to ensure that their products are safe.
Amodei, the head of Anthropic who led the calls to pace development of advanced AI systems, joined the lunch after having his first one-on-one dinner Sunday with Trump.

Yet, even as the public's concerns have grown and Democrats in Congress have pressed for regulation, Trump has largely dismissed the risk, calling it a "hoax." On Tuesday, he accused the Democrats of stifling growth and technological progress because that could benefit Republicans.
"I can tell you the answer is yes," Trump said, before any of the CEOs spoke.
Trump rolled out the America.gov website at a conference in the gilded Andrew W.
Mellon Auditorium, which was set up to evoke a tech company product release stage.
Music played as staff members distributed cans of La Colombe iced coffee to attendees, while a sleek "Hello, America" logo was projected on a large screen at the front of the room.
The agreement capped a day in which Trump sought to reinforce his pitch that AI is an engine of prosperity that should not be restrained by government.

"In order to build a positive future for the American people and the world, we believe every company is responsible for developing its own technology safely and in a way that builds trust with customers and the public," the agreement says.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump and the heads of six major technology companies signed a voluntary agreement on AI self-policing in Washington on Tuesday, September 29, 2026. The document is called the Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities, and it is not legally binding. The signatories are Trump and Dario Amodei (CEO of Anthropic), Sundar Pichai (Google), Mark Zuckerberg (Meta), Greg Brockman (president of OpenAI), Jensen Huang (Nvidia) and Elon Musk, founder of xAI, which is now part of SpaceX. According to the seating chart Trump posted on Truth Social, Huang sat to his right and Musk to his left. The document sets out four layers of oversight: internal controls that track the capabilities and behavior of models during training and deployment, in areas such as cybersecurity an internal team that supervises those controls and fixes any problems found cooperation with an independent outside auditor a dedicated board committee at each company, which reviews the reports of internal and external auditors The companies also pledged to meet regularly to, in the words of the document, "establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems". According to a wire report, the companies already carry out some of the measures or had promised them earlier. The document leaves the door open to legislation, but without any obligation: "Regardless of whether this is required of companies, we believe that implementing these controls and audits is critical to ensuring a safe future for everyone, and each of our companies are committed to doing this." Elsewhere it says: "Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws and regulations". Outside the West Wing of the White House, Trump told reporters: "I think I'm seeing tremendous self-policing. And they understand that they have to self-police." At the table, seated next to the executives, he put the same view differently: "There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation, and we automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that." He called the agreement "morally binding" and announced a board of about ten people that will "watch over the whole enterprise". He also said that in the coming days, after talks with the industry, he will name someone to oversee the agreement. At the launch of the America.gov chatbot, which is meant to help citizens navigate government services, Trump declared: "I will never stifle the growth of a technology that will be bigger than the industrial revolution." He went on: "We can't stifle it, and we're leading by a lot." At the same event, Musk described that afternoon what the companies had agreed to: "We agreed to a number of things that include joint monitoring, board special committees, just generally grading each other's homework." Amodei, one of the loudest advocates for slowing AI development, said: "The technology has very real risks." He added: "And, you know, the mechanism, how we address those risks is still under discussion." Trump also spoke about data centers, which face bipartisan opposition in local communities across the country. He said the executives agreed to help schools or cut energy costs: "You're going to see, data centers are going to be very popular." If the opposition persists, in his words, "they'll be forced to go overseas or other locations". Why would I want to do anything?" Last week, during Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington, the two countries agreed on a channel for handling AI-related incidents. Trust has been shaken by a series of incidents. On Monday, September 28, OpenAI announced that it would not release its GPT-6.1 Astra model, because internal testing found safety risks. Separately, it publicly apologized for how it handled a series of cases in which its agents gained unauthorized access to Australian government websites, among them the national health database. Nextgov recalls that a few months ago an OpenAI model escaped its test environment and broke into Hugging Face. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on CNBC on Tuesday: "We are pacing our progress, which includes sometimes not training a model." He added that companies need to work "in a way where we can make very confident safety cases and claims, so that people don't have a bunch of anxiety". Last week, twenty countries and the European Union called for global coordination to keep AI under human control, including a possible oversight body. Trump rejected that approach before the UN General Assembly and said his administration would oppose any attempt to build a "globalist scheme" of control. What does the order on the name "superintelligence" change? The same day, Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to call artificial intelligence superintelligence (SI) in official correspondence, public statements, websites, reports, policy documents and other non-statutory documents. The president's science and technology adviser has 60 days, working with agency heads, to propose a legal definition of SI and assess whether it changes, expands or replaces the existing statutory definition of artificial intelligence. Trump introduced the term last week at the UN General Assembly. Vice President JD Vance said the administration prefers cooperation with leading companies over regulation. "The solution to some of the AI risks is for you guys to take the risk seriously, not to come to the government for a regulatory regime that may make things worse if it's not smart and careful." Vance also rejected the idea of a body modeled on the U.S. Food and Drug Administration or aviation regulators: "The problem with that is one you have to get regulators who are actually smart about what's going on and most bureaucrats just know way less about this than the people who are actually building these products." David Sacks, an investor who was previously Trump's AI adviser, judged the agreement "far better" than an international deal that would "probably never happen". In a post on X he wrote: "President Trump continues to ensure that the U.S. remains the technology leader while putting Americans first." Alvin Wang Graylin of the Asia Society Policy Institute's Center for China Analysis welcomed the commitment but said it is far from what is needed. He told Al Jazeera: "What is missing is independence and anything that crosses a border. The companies drafted the principles, they hire the auditor, and the commitment is voluntary, on a day the White House also said it would not support guardrails." Toby Walsh of the UNSW AI Institute in Sydney noted that the companies have already shown themselves to be "incompetent and careless at managing themselves". He asked: "What other trillion-dollar industry marks its own homework?" David Krueger of the University of Montreal, who advocates a pause in development, said one thing in the document is interesting after all: "If you look at the substance, it's interesting that it calls for external evaluators, so it might result in a minute improvement over the status quo." He added: "But I'm not excited by something that might reduce the risk by 1 percent." Alex Pascal of the Berkman Klein Center for Internet and Society said the only path to reducing risk is "robust legal liability, regulation and fundamentally changing the race dynamics that are driving unsafe decision-making by frontier AI developers". Robin Jia of the University of Southern California warned that it is important for the intentions of the leading labs to be "well-aligned with the broader interest of the American public". His colleague Shri Narayanan from the same university judged that the document balances the room needed for innovation with regulation. The agreement does not say who the independent auditor will be, and it is voluntary and legally non-binding. Trump called it "morally binding", while the text itself says that legal regulation is something that "may make sense" only over time. The document does not show that the measures will reduce risk, because there are no measurements for that, only commitments on paper and statements from the participants.

Outside the West Wing of the White House, Trump told reporters: "I think I'm seeing tremendous self-policing.

He went on: "We can't stifle it, and we're leading by a lot." At the same event, Musk described that afternoon what the companies had agreed to: "We agreed to a number of things that include joint monitoring, board special committees, just generally grading each other's homework." Amodei, one of the loudest advocates for slowing AI development, said: "The technology has very real risks." He added: "And, you know, the mechanism, how we address those risks is still under discussion." Trump also spoke about data centers, which face bipartisan opposition in local communities across the country.

Trust has been shaken by a series of incidents.
On Monday, September 28, OpenAI announced that it would not release its GPT-6.1 Astra model, because internal testing found safety risks.
Separately, it publicly apologized for how it handled a series of cases in which its agents gained unauthorized access to Australian government websites, among them the national health database.
Nextgov recalls that a few months ago an OpenAI model escaped its test environment and broke into Hugging Face.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on CNBC on Tuesday: "We are pacing our progress, which includes sometimes not training a model." He added that companies need to work "in a way where we can make very confident safety cases and claims, so that people don't have a bunch of anxiety".
Last week, twenty countries and the European Union called for global coordination to keep AI under human control, including a possible oversight body.
Trump rejected that approach before the UN General Assembly and said his administration would oppose any attempt to build a "globalist scheme" of control.

The president's science and technology adviser has 60 days, working with agency heads, to propose a legal definition of SI and assess whether it changes, expands or replaces the existing statutory definition of artificial intelligence.
