extraction.body: President Donald Trump declared at the United Nations on Tuesday that the US government will no longer use the term "artificial intelligence" in official documents, replacing it with "Super Intelligence" because he believes the word "artificial" makes the technology sound fake. Speaking before the General Assembly, Trump said the change would take effect immediately across all federal paperwork and expressed hope that other nations would follow suit. "The United States also rejects any scheme for globalist control of Artificial Intelligence, being spoken of so much now. Here and after officially called Super Intelligence. Changing the name," he said. The president argued that the existing terminology undersells the technology. "The use of 'Artificial' makes it sound fake. It makes intelligence sound fake, and it is not fake. It's actually amazing, the opposite of what they report," he told the assembly. Trump added: "From this day forward, all United States documents, and hopefully the world's, will be changed to use the much more accurate term 'Super' as opposed to 'Artificial.' So it's Super Intelligence." The announcement caps a days-long push by the president to rebrand the technology. On Saturday, he posted on Truth Social asking followers to weigh in on alternatives, floating "Superior Intelligence" and "Extreme Intelligence" as possibilities before settling on "Super Intelligence." The post claimed that "many people" consider the phrase "artificial intelligence" to be "inaccurate, and very ineloquent." The rebranding creates a potential collision with established AI research terminology. In academic and industry circles, "superintelligence" refers to a hypothetical future system whose intellectual capabilities would surpass human performance across virtually all domains — a threshold no existing AI model has reached. By applying the label to all AI systems, the administration's usage would stretch the term far beyond its conventional meaning. The shift comes as governments worldwide debate how to govern increasingly capable systems, with 22 countries backing a declaration on Monday calling for AI to remain under human direction, oversight and control. The United States and China were not signatories. The terminology change aligns with the administration's broader posture of accelerating AI development rather than constraining it. In June, Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to promote AI innovation and security while explicitly barring mandatory licensing or pre-clearance requirements for AI models. A separate June memorandum instructed national security agencies to speed up adoption of advanced AI systems and make frontier models more readily available to defense and intelligence professionals. White House policy documents from 2026 describe AI as a transformative technology comparable to the Industrial Revolution and identify US leadership in the field as an economic and national security priority. The administration has also signaled it will challenge state-level efforts to regulate AI, with Trump previously indicating plans to sue American states that attempt to impose their own rules on the technology. The rebranding lands amid intensifying debate over AI safety. A UN-backed scientific panel has urged governments to implement safeguards around advanced AI without waiting for complete scientific certainty about potential risks. Meanwhile, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for a slowdown in AI development after a former researcher at the company accused the industry of "gambling with our lives." Trump has consistently rejected such cautionary approaches, arguing that the United States should prioritize speed over precaution. His administration has framed AI leadership as essential to maintaining competitive advantage, expanding American AI infrastructure, research, national-security applications and exports. The president is not the first administration official to stumble over AI terminology. Last year, Education Secretary Linda McMahon repeatedly referred to the technology as "A1" — like the steak sauce brand — during a public event. For Trump, the name change is more than bureaucratic semantics. It arrives at a moment when governments are simultaneously wrestling with what increasingly capable AI should be called, how it should be developed, and ultimately how much human control should be retained over systems that can operate with limited intervention. "The United States also rejects any scheme for globalist control of Artificial Intelligence, being spoken of so much now. Here and after officially called Super Intelligence. Changing the name," he said.

The president argued that the existing terminology undersells the technology. "The use of 'Artificial' makes it sound fake. It makes intelligence sound fake, and it is not fake. It's actually amazing, the opposite of what they report," he told the assembly.

Trump added: "From this day forward, all United States documents, and hopefully the world's, will be changed to use the much more accurate term 'Super' as opposed to 'Artificial.' So it's Super Intelligence."

The announcement caps a days-long push by the president to rebrand the technology. On Saturday, he posted on Truth Social asking followers to weigh in on alternatives, floating "Superior Intelligence" and "Extreme Intelligence" as possibilities before settling on "Super Intelligence." The post claimed that "many people" consider the phrase "artificial intelligence" to be "inaccurate, and very ineloquent."

The rebranding creates a potential collision with established AI research terminology. In academic and industry circles, "superintelligence" refers to a hypothetical future system whose intellectual capabilities would surpass human performance across virtually all domains — a threshold no existing AI model has reached.

By applying the label to all AI systems, the administration's usage would stretch the term far beyond its conventional meaning. The shift comes as governments worldwide debate how to govern increasingly capable systems, with 22 countries backing a declaration on Monday calling for AI to remain under human direction, oversight and control. The United States and China were not signatories.

The terminology change aligns with the administration's broader posture of accelerating AI development rather than constraining it. In June, Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to promote AI innovation and security while explicitly barring mandatory licensing or pre-clearance requirements for AI models.

A separate June memorandum instructed national security agencies to speed up adoption of advanced AI systems and make frontier models more readily available to defense and intelligence professionals. White House policy documents from 2026 describe AI as a transformative technology comparable to the Industrial Revolution and identify US leadership in the field as an economic and national security priority.

The administration has also signaled it will challenge state-level efforts to regulate AI, with Trump previously indicating plans to sue American states that attempt to impose their own rules on the technology.

The rebranding lands amid intensifying debate over AI safety. A UN-backed scientific panel has urged governments to implement safeguards around advanced AI without waiting for complete scientific certainty about potential risks. Meanwhile, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for a slowdown in AI development after a former researcher at the company accused the industry of "gambling with our lives."

Trump has consistently rejected such cautionary approaches, arguing that the United States should prioritize speed over precaution. His administration has framed AI leadership as essential to maintaining competitive advantage, expanding American AI infrastructure, research, national-security applications and exports.

The president is not the first administration official to stumble over AI terminology. Last year, Education Secretary Linda McMahon repeatedly referred to the technology as "A1" — like the steak sauce brand — during a public event.

For Trump, the name change is more than bureaucratic semantics. It arrives at a moment when governments are simultaneously wrestling with what increasingly capable AI should be called, how it should be developed, and ultimately how much human control should be retained over systems that can operate with limited intervention.

coreStoryFacts.text: Trump signed the executive order after a luncheon he hosted at the White House with tech CEOs and government officials to discuss what he’s now officially calling Super Intelligence.

In brief public remarks after the meeting, flanked by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, and surrounded by other attendees, Trump called the lunch “very productive” and “extremely friendly.” “There’s a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation,” Trump said.

“And we automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that.” On the local level, where tech companies have faced the most hurdles in building out massive data centers needed to run their services, Trump says the firms will “work to make the community happy” by providing resources and economic support they may need.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump declared at the United Nations on Tuesday that the US government will no longer use the term "artificial intelligence" in official documents, replacing it with "Super Intelligence" because he believes the word "artificial" makes the technology sound fake. Speaking before the General Assembly, Trump said the change would take effect immediately across all federal paperwork and expressed hope that other nations would follow suit. "The United States also rejects any scheme for globalist control of Artificial Intelligence, being spoken of so much now. Here and after officially called Super Intelligence. Changing the name," he said. The president argued that the existing terminology undersells the technology. "The use of 'Artificial' makes it sound fake. It makes intelligence sound fake, and it is not fake. It's actually amazing, the opposite of what they report," he told the assembly. Trump added: "From this day forward, all United States documents, and hopefully the world's, will be changed to use the much more accurate term 'Super' as opposed to 'Artificial.' So it's Super Intelligence." The announcement caps a days-long push by the president to rebrand the technology. On Saturday, he posted on Truth Social asking followers to weigh in on alternatives, floating "Superior Intelligence" and "Extreme Intelligence" as possibilities before settling on "Super Intelligence." The post claimed that "many people" consider the phrase "artificial intelligence" to be "inaccurate, and very ineloquent." The rebranding creates a potential collision with established AI research terminology. In academic and industry circles, "superintelligence" refers to a hypothetical future system whose intellectual capabilities would surpass human performance across virtually all domains — a threshold no existing AI model has reached. By applying the label to all AI systems, the administration's usage would stretch the term far beyond its conventional meaning. The shift comes as governments worldwide debate how to govern increasingly capable systems, with 22 countries backing a declaration on Monday calling for AI to remain under human direction, oversight and control. The United States and China were not signatories. The terminology change aligns with the administration's broader posture of accelerating AI development rather than constraining it. In June, Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to promote AI innovation and security while explicitly barring mandatory licensing or pre-clearance requirements for AI models. A separate June memorandum instructed national security agencies to speed up adoption of advanced AI systems and make frontier models more readily available to defense and intelligence professionals. White House policy documents from 2026 describe AI as a transformative technology comparable to the Industrial Revolution and identify US leadership in the field as an economic and national security priority. The administration has also signaled it will challenge state-level efforts to regulate AI, with Trump previously indicating plans to sue American states that attempt to impose their own rules on the technology. The rebranding lands amid intensifying debate over AI safety. A UN-backed scientific panel has urged governments to implement safeguards around advanced AI without waiting for complete scientific certainty about potential risks. Meanwhile, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for a slowdown in AI development after a former researcher at the company accused the industry of "gambling with our lives." Trump has consistently rejected such cautionary approaches, arguing that the United States should prioritize speed over precaution. His administration has framed AI leadership as essential to maintaining competitive advantage, expanding American AI infrastructure, research, national-security applications and exports. The president is not the first administration official to stumble over AI terminology. Last year, Education Secretary Linda McMahon repeatedly referred to the technology as "A1" — like the steak sauce brand — during a public event. For Trump, the name change is more than bureaucratic semantics. It arrives at a moment when governments are simultaneously wrestling with what increasingly capable AI should be called, how it should be developed, and ultimately how much human control should be retained over systems that can operate with limited intervention. Zuckerberg described the agreement as a starting point for developing standards across the industry. Tesla and SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk said the arrangement effectively meant companies would be “grading each other’s homework”, rather than assessing their own performance. The White House gathering came amid growing political pressure in the US over the rapid development of AI. Lawmakers are facing increasing calls to address concerns that the technology could displace workers and have wider social consequences. Data centres, which require large amounts of electricity and water, have become a contentious issue in several US communities, with residents raising concerns over utility costs and pressure on local resources. passages: OpenAI is responding to Meta’s buzzy Muse AI with agentic helpers of its own: Dots.

passages: OpenAI introduced Dots at its DevDay 2026 developer conference.
According to the company, they're always-on agents that take over ongoing tasks, keep an eye on projects, and reach out when something needs the user's attention.
Each Dot has its own cloud computer with a browser, so it can work around the clock.
There it does research, analyzes data, writes documents, or builds software through Codex.
Technically, Dots are similar to Meta's Muse agent, which launched three weeks earlier.
OpenAI is going further for businesses with specialized Dots that take on fixed roles inside an organization.
These get their own identity, their own credentials, and, if the company wants, computers supplied by IT.
OpenAI says it has tested them internally in purchasing, invoice processing, email marketing, customer support, and contract management.
The rollout starts with pilot projects at individual companies.
In one internal case, OpenAI says a Dot followed a bug reported in Slack all the way to a working new build.
For an early tester, the agent spotted a forgotten invoice, prepared it, and sent it once the tester approved.
Each user gets one Dot at launch, but OpenAI's long-term plan is whole teams of Dots working together.
Alongside them, OpenAI is releasing GPT-6.1 Sol, a cheaper model.
A Dot can also use saved passwords without the model ever seeing them.
Safeguards are supposed to block malicious instructions, and a monitoring system can pause or stop the work if safety concerns come up.
An Activity View shows what the Dot is working on, including tasks running in the background.
OpenAI admits Dots can make mistakes and recommends double-checking any results that carry real consequences.
Plugins let a Dot connect to more than 4,000 apps and move several projects forward at the same time.
OpenAI says the agent learns from feedback how its user works and what they consider a good result.
Users can reach their Dot through chat or voice calls in ChatGPT, and also in Slack and Microsoft Teams.
The Dot keeps its context across all of these channels, OpenAI says.
OpenAI calls this "proactive research." In this mode, the agent only uses read-only tools, which can't send messages, change content, or control a browser or computer.
For active tasks, a set of ground rules decides when a Dot acts alone and when it checks in first.
Custom Rules let users allow individual actions, require approval for them, or ban them outright.
OpenAI says an automated check reviews any action that touches accounts or shares information against those rules before it goes through.
Sensitive tasks like changing a password always stay with the human.
OpenAI's demos also include everyday errands, like ordering food by text message.
The company says that feature is coming soon.
Users on personal plans decide for themselves whether their Dot's conversations and work can be used for training.
OpenAI also says it doesn't train directly on the background research or the notes a Dot keeps for itself.
For now, Pro subscribers can only use Dots outside the European Economic Area, Switzerland, and the UK.
Business Premium customers get them in all supported regions, while Enterprise, Edu, and Healthcare customers can try a beta once their admins switch it on.
Users set up their Dot in the desktop app or browser first, and after that it's also available on mobile.

There it does research, analyzes data, writes documents, or builds software through Codex.
Technically, Dots are similar to Meta's Muse agent, which launched three weeks earlier.
OpenAI is going further for businesses with specialized Dots that take on fixed roles inside an organization.
These get their own identity, their own credentials, and, if the company wants, computers supplied by IT.
OpenAI says it has tested them internally in purchasing, invoice processing, email marketing, customer support, and contract management.
The rollout starts with pilot projects at individual companies.
In one internal case, OpenAI says a Dot followed a bug reported in Slack all the way to a working new build.
For an early tester, the agent spotted a forgotten invoice, prepared it, and sent it once the tester approved.
Each user gets one Dot at launch, but OpenAI's long-term plan is whole teams of Dots working together.
Alongside them, OpenAI is releasing GPT-6.1 Sol, a cheaper model.
A Dot can also use saved passwords without the model ever seeing them.
Safeguards are supposed to block malicious instructions, and a monitoring system can pause or stop the work if safety concerns come up.
An Activity View shows what the Dot is working on, including tasks running in the background.
OpenAI admits Dots can make mistakes and recommends double-checking any results that carry real consequences.
Plugins let a Dot connect to more than 4,000 apps and move several projects forward at the same time.
OpenAI says the agent learns from feedback how its user works and what they consider a good result.
Users can reach their Dot through chat or voice calls in ChatGPT, and also in Slack and Microsoft Teams.
The Dot keeps its context across all of these channels, OpenAI says.
OpenAI calls this "proactive research." In this mode, the agent only uses read-only tools, which can't send messages, change content, or control a browser or computer.
For active tasks, a set of ground rules decides when a Dot acts alone and when it checks in first.
Custom Rules let users allow individual actions, require approval for them, or ban them outright.
OpenAI says an automated check reviews any action that touches accounts or shares information against those rules before it goes through.
Sensitive tasks like changing a password always stay with the human.
OpenAI's demos also include everyday errands, like ordering food by text message.
The company says that feature is coming soon.
Users on personal plans decide for themselves whether their Dot's conversations and work can be used for training.
OpenAI also says it doesn't train directly on the background research or the notes a Dot keeps for itself.
For now, Pro subscribers can only use Dots outside the European Economic Area, Switzerland, and the UK.
Business Premium customers get them in all supported regions, while Enterprise, Edu, and Healthcare customers can try a beta once their admins switch it on.
Users set up their Dot in the desktop app or browser first, and after that it's also available on mobile.

First, Anthropic launched its Claude Opus 5.5 model last week that not only exceeded the capabilities of its Fable 5.1 model but also beat OpenAI's reigning apex model, GPT-6 Astra, on most benchmarks . In fact, Claude Opus 5.5 on a medium intensity beat GPT-6 Astra on max for a fifth of the cost per task on OSWorld 2.0 Offline. OpenAI did try to put up a fight by debuting GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna models. However, as we had noted at the time , while GPT-6 Luna is cheaper than even the off-peak API pricing for the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash model, which offers input at $0.15 per 1 million tokens and output at $0.60 per 1 million tokens , DeepSeek V4.1 Flash still scored 74.2 on DeepSWE v1.1 vs. GPT-6 Luna's score of around 67. What's more, Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 is currently leading the scoreboard when it comes to the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with a score of 58 vs. 48 for GPT-6 Sol. Additionally, on Monday, Anthropic released the newest iteration of its workhorse model, Claude Sonnet 5.5, which scored 56 on Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index , placing it behind Claude Opus 5.5 but above GPT-6 Astra and miles above GPT-6 Sol. What's more, according to Anthropic, the Sonnet 5.5 is around 30 percent faster and cheaper than the Sonnet 5.0 on most tasks even though it is priced at the same $2 per 1 million tokens of input and $12 per 1 million tokens of output . And to make matters worse, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday that OpenAI has apparently scrapped its GPT-6.1 Astra model after it showed a higher proclivity for engaging in deception, while breaking regression testing, hallucinating tool calls, ignoring user guardrails, and failing to follow basic instructions. And, on the consumer front, Meta's new personal AI agent, Muse, has been breaking adoption records, far outpacing the initial uptake of ChatGPT and Gemini apps . In what is a rare bit of positive news, however, Axios has just reported that OpenAI's annual recurring revenue (ARR) is now close to $70 billion ($68 billion to be exact) after growing by over 70 percent since the beginning of Q3 2026. For reference, Anthropic's ARR hovered near $65 billion in August . The last few weeks are an apt reminder of how quickly the script can be flipped Though today's DevDay will be interesting for sure, unlimited Sol & Luna for Pro plans just isn't going to make up for halved Astra limits, and a new $500 tier is a bit silly when their models are… As for what you can expect during Sam Altman's keynote address scheduled for 10:00 a.m. PT, OpenAI will likely unveil personal AI agents called Dots. According to the leaker M1, " you can text it, call it, Slack it, and email it, and it can buy things for you with your approval ." Each Dot also gets its own 3D avatar that you can design. Do note that OpenAI had teased an always-on agent, called "o ," over the weekend. It is unclear if Dot and "o" are the same product or represent entirely different launches. OpenAI has given each Dot access to its own cloud computer (VM) and browser. When combined with the access to a plethora of apps via plugins, Dots become a veritable productivity powerhouse. According to OpenAI, you can message or call Dots in ChatGPT on desktop, web, and mobile. They can also message you with progress, questions, or decisions that need your input. You can also message your Dot in Slack and Teams, with support for texting expected to land soon. "Each Dot works on its own cloud computer, while your computer and its contents stay separate unless you choose to connect it. For signing into supported websites, Dots can use saved passwords without exposing them to the model." Also, the AI lab is partnering with Amazon to host Dots on AWS. According to Altman, "the cache input costs [$0.10 per 1 million tokens] are a 95% discount on standard input. So this makes it much cheaper for agents to reuse context, iterate on solutions, and work through longer tasks." According to OpenAI, the model scores higher than Anthropic's Opus 5.5 on GDP.pdf, which measures how accurately models answer professional questions using complex PDF documents, including tables, charts, diagrams, and fine-print details. It also approaches GPT‑6 Astra’s performance on the benchmark at roughly one-fifth the cost per task. On AutomationBench, which measures whether agents correctly complete multi-step business workflows, GPT‑6.1 Sol scores 2.2 percent above Opus 5.5's score at medium reasoning effort, at roughly a third of the cost. On OSWorld 2.0’s offline set, which evaluates agents on demanding computer-use workflows, GPT‑6.1 Sol comes within 2.1 percentage points of Astra’s score at maximum reasoning effort at roughly one-seventh the cost per task. According to OpenAI, GPT‑6.1 Sol also improves factual accuracy on difficult prompts, with the largest factuality improvement over GPT‑6 Sol coming on low reasoning effort, where it reduces the share of responses containing a factual error from 11.4 percent to 7.7 percent, with the overall error rate remaining within 1.9 percentage points of GPT‑6 Astra’s, at less than one-fifth the cost per task. And, if you were wondering why OpenAI would launch a new Sol model just a few days after the GPT-6 Sol, it is intended to paper over the embarrassment caused last week. OpenAI's Ultrafast offers up to 8× faster token generation (300 tokens per second) in Codex and up to 6x in the API. Leaked tidbits in recent days had indicated that this tier would be powered by Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine, but OpenAI has yet to confirm it. GPT‑6 Astra Ultrafast is available today in the API⁠ and in ChatGPT Work and Codex⁠ on Pro 500 and Enterprise plans, while GPT‑6.1 Sol Ultrafast is expected to land soon. It costs an insane $60 per 1 million tokens of input and $300 per 1 million tokens of output though! coreStoryFacts.text: OpenAI is responding to Meta’s buzzy Muse AI with agentic helpers of its own: Dots.

During its DevDay keynote on Tuesday, OpenAI announced that Dots will serve as always-on AI assistants that can “do nearly anything” across connected apps in the background while learning your preferences over time.
Dots also learn while they work, allowing them to personalize their output and come up with other tasks to complete “before you even think to ask,” according to OpenAI.
OpenAI says Dots come with “built-in rules for when to act independently,” but you can set custom ones that block certain actions or dictate when it should ask for permission.
OpenAI is also testing a feature that lets companies create “specialist” Dots to handle specific roles inside organizations.
The company’s capable GPT-6 Astra model powers Dots, which use their own cloud computer to access a web browser and more than 4,000 supported apps.
It will soon be able to talk to you over text message as well. [Video: OpenAI Dots] For now, you can only create one Dot, though OpenAI plans to allow users to deploy multiple agents at once.
Dots can also connect to Microsoft Teams and Slack, where they will carry over the context from your sessions on other apps and devices.
As an example, OpenAI says a developer working on an app could ask their Dot to use customer feedback to build and test updates, while presenting them with a video showing its changes.
OpenAI notes that conversations with your Dot won’t count toward ChatGPT usage limits.
OpenAI today announced the launch of "Dots" to compete with Meta 's popular Muse agent.

The agents learn from feedback over time, and OpenAI says they can work on the user's goals "24/7" and connect to over 4,000 apps.
Conversations with the agent don't count toward ChatGPT usage limits, but tasks will use plan allowances.
Dots can be set up in the ChatGPT desktop app and accessed in the mobile app afterward.
Users can communicate with Dots through ChatGPT or other apps like Slack or Teams, and options to text Dots are planned.
Dots follow ChatGPT's permissions and support custom rules for which tasks require approval.
Users can create a "primary dot" and name it starting today, with teams of Dots coming later.
Dots are rolling out for Pro, Business Premium, and Enterprise plans in select markets, with other users to get access soon.

sources.title: OpenAI launches always-on Dots agents to rival Meta's Muse - the-decoder.com
passages: OpenAI introduced Dots at its DevDay 2026 developer conference.
According to the company, they're always-on agents that take over ongoing tasks, keep an eye on projects, and reach out when something needs the user's attention.
Each Dot has its own cloud computer with a browser, so it can work around the clock.
There it does research, analyzes data, writes documents, or builds software through Codex.
Technically, Dots are similar to Meta's Muse agent, which launched three weeks earlier.
OpenAI is going further for businesses with specialized Dots that take on fixed roles inside an organization.
These get their own identity, their own credentials, and, if the company wants, computers supplied by IT.
OpenAI says it has tested them internally in purchasing, invoice processing, email marketing, customer support, and contract management.
The rollout starts with pilot projects at individual companies.
In one internal case, OpenAI says a Dot followed a bug reported in Slack all the way to a working new build.
For an early tester, the agent spotted a forgotten invoice, prepared it, and sent it once the tester approved.
Each user gets one Dot at launch, but OpenAI's long-term plan is whole teams of Dots working together.
Alongside them, OpenAI is releasing GPT-6.1 Sol, a cheaper model.
A Dot can also use saved passwords without the model ever seeing them.
Safeguards are supposed to block malicious instructions, and a monitoring system can pause or stop the work if safety concerns come up.
An Activity View shows what the Dot is working on, including tasks running in the background.
OpenAI admits Dots can make mistakes and recommends double-checking any results that carry real consequences.
Plugins let a Dot connect to more than 4,000 apps and move several projects forward at the same time.
OpenAI says the agent learns from feedback how its user works and what they consider a good result.
Users can reach their Dot through chat or voice calls in ChatGPT, and also in Slack and Microsoft Teams.
The Dot keeps its context across all of these channels, OpenAI says.
OpenAI calls this "proactive research." In this mode, the agent only uses read-only tools, which can't send messages, change content, or control a browser or computer.
For active tasks, a set of ground rules decides when a Dot acts alone and when it checks in first.
Custom Rules let users allow individual actions, require approval for them, or ban them outright.
OpenAI says an automated check reviews any action that touches accounts or shares information against those rules before it goes through.
Sensitive tasks like changing a password always stay with the human.
OpenAI's demos also include everyday errands, like ordering food by text message.
The company says that feature is coming soon.
Users on personal plans decide for themselves whether their Dot's conversations and work can be used for training.
OpenAI also says it doesn't train directly on the background research or the notes a Dot keeps for itself.
For now, Pro subscribers can only use Dots outside the European Economic Area, Switzerland, and the UK.
Business Premium customers get them in all supported regions, while Enterprise, Edu, and Healthcare customers can try a beta once their admins switch it on.
Users set up their Dot in the desktop app or browser first, and after that it's also available on mobile.

passages: OpenAI is finally delivering on the hype that it attempted to build over the past few weeks for its DevDay 2026, replete with over 20 distinct product launches, albeit complicated by an evolving competitive environment where Anthropic has again taken an apparent lead by launching the eminently stellar Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 AI models.
PT, OpenAI will likely unveil personal AI agents called Dots.

In what is a rare bit of positive news, however, Axios has just reported that OpenAI's annual recurring revenue (ARR) is now close to $70 billion ($68 billion to be exact) after growing by over 70 percent since the beginning of Q3 2026.
For reference, Anthropic's ARR hovered near $65 billion in August .
As expected, OpenAI has just unveiled Dots , your personal, always-on AI agents powered by GPT-6 Astra.
With support for OpenAI's plugins, Dots can connect to over 4,000 apps, including ChatGPT, Slack, and Teams.

Also, we can't but help notice that Dots appear to be geared more towards enterprises, which should give Meta's Muse a relatively unhindered path for now to dominate the consumer-oriented personal AI agent space.
The fact that the Dot is only available on the Pro tiers while Meta Muse is free up to a limit will also skew the uptake.
Do note that OpenAI had teased an always-on agent, called "o ," over the weekend.

extraction.body: OpenAI is finally delivering on the hype that it attempted to build over the past few weeks for its DevDay 2026, replete with over 20 distinct product launches, albeit complicated by an evolving competitive environment where Anthropic has again taken an apparent lead by launching the eminently stellar Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 AI models. OpenAI has suffered a series of setbacks recently. First, Anthropic launched its Claude Opus 5.5 model last week that not only exceeded the capabilities of its Fable 5.1 model but also beat OpenAI's reigning apex model, GPT-6 Astra, on most benchmarks . In fact, Claude Opus 5.5 on a medium intensity beat GPT-6 Astra on max for a fifth of the cost per task on OSWorld 2.0 Offline. OpenAI did try to put up a fight by debuting GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna models. However, as we had noted at the time , while GPT-6 Luna is cheaper than even the off-peak API pricing for the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash model, which offers input at $0.15 per 1 million tokens and output at $0.60 per 1 million tokens , DeepSeek V4.1 Flash still scored 74.2 on DeepSWE v1.1 vs. GPT-6 Luna's score of around 67. What's more, Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 is currently leading the scoreboard when it comes to the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with a score of 58 vs. 48 for GPT-6 Sol. Additionally, on Monday, Anthropic released the newest iteration of its workhorse model, Claude Sonnet 5.5, which scored 56 on Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index , placing it behind Claude Opus 5.5 but above GPT-6 Astra and miles above GPT-6 Sol. What's more, according to Anthropic, the Sonnet 5.5 is around 30 percent faster and cheaper than the Sonnet 5.0 on most tasks even though it is priced at the same $2 per 1 million tokens of input and $12 per 1 million tokens of output . And to make matters worse, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday that OpenAI has apparently scrapped its GPT-6.1 Astra model after it showed a higher proclivity for engaging in deception, while breaking regression testing, hallucinating tool calls, ignoring user guardrails, and failing to follow basic instructions. And, on the consumer front, Meta's new personal AI agent, Muse, has been breaking adoption records, far outpacing the initial uptake of ChatGPT and Gemini apps . In what is a rare bit of positive news, however, Axios has just reported that OpenAI's annual recurring revenue (ARR) is now close to $70 billion ($68 billion to be exact) after growing by over 70 percent since the beginning of Q3 2026. For reference, Anthropic's ARR hovered near $65 billion in August . The last few weeks are an apt reminder of how quickly the script can be flipped Though today's DevDay will be interesting for sure, unlimited Sol & Luna for Pro plans just isn't going to make up for halved Astra limits, and a new $500 tier is a bit silly when their models are… As for what you can expect during Sam Altman's keynote address scheduled for 10:00 a.m. PT, OpenAI will likely unveil personal AI agents called Dots. According to the leaker M1, " you can text it, call it, Slack it, and email it, and it can buy things for you with your approval ." Each Dot also gets its own 3D avatar that you can design. Do note that OpenAI had teased an always-on agent, called "o ," over the weekend. It is unclear if Dot and "o" are the same product or represent entirely different launches. Your dot is ready to meet you. pic.twitter.com/HyC9ZAztOm As expected, OpenAI has just unveiled Dots , your personal, always-on AI agents powered by GPT-6 Astra. With support for OpenAI's plugins, Dots can connect to over 4,000 apps, including ChatGPT, Slack, and Teams. You can interact with Dots via text or hop onto a call. OpenAI has given each Dot access to its own cloud computer (VM) and browser. When combined with the access to a plethora of apps via plugins, Dots become a veritable productivity powerhouse. According to OpenAI, you can message or call Dots in ChatGPT on desktop, web, and mobile. They can also message you with progress, questions, or decisions that need your input. You can also message your Dot in Slack and Teams, with support for texting expected to land soon. "Each Dot works on its own cloud computer, while your computer and its contents stay separate unless you choose to connect it. For signing into supported websites, Dots can use saved passwords without exposing them to the model." OpenAI also assures that it "does not use content from ChatGPT Business, Enterprise, or Edu workspaces to improve our models by default," while those holding personal ChatGPT plans can opt out at anytime. In what is a big deal, OpenAI says that it is also bringing Dots to Microsoft Agent 365, allowing businesses to manage these agents via tools that they already use. Also, the AI lab is partnering with Amazon to host Dots on AWS. Finally, OpenAI says that Dots are rolling out today in ChatGPT to Pro and Business Premium users in all markets excluding the European Economic Area, Switzerland, and the UK . Enterprise users (including Edu and Healthcare) can try the beta when their workspace admin enables it. Also, your first Dot is included in your Pro or Business Premium plan at no extra cost. Moreover, for the next month, your Dots usage won’t count toward your plan's allowances (conversations only and not actual tasks). OpenAI’s new AI agent Dot failed to respond during its first live demo prompting the presenter to say “I guess Dot’s having a slow morning.” I just added to my $META position. pic.twitter.com/dzFDHBYuXA We should note though that Dot's debut was not without a hitch, with the agent failing to respond during OpenAI's demo. Also, we can't but help notice that Dots appear to be geared more towards enterprises, which should give Meta's Muse a relatively unhindered path for now to dominate the consumer-oriented personal AI agent space. The fact that the Dot is only available on the Pro tiers while Meta Muse is free up to a limit will also skew the uptake. GPT-6.1 Sol replaces GPT-6 Sol after just 7 days. It scores 1 point below GPT-6 Astra in the Intelligence Index at less than one quarter of the Cost per Task Pricing matches GPT-6 Sol at $2/$10 per million input/output tokens, except that the cache read discount rises from 90%… pic.twitter.com/LcuAxgLSBj OpenAI has just announced GPT-6.1 Sol , its new workhorse model that supposedly offers "near-Astra level intelligence at a fifth of the price" on DeepSWE v1.1, which evaluates complex software-engineering tasks in real codebases. According to Altman, "the cache input costs [$0.10 per 1 million tokens] are a 95% discount on standard input. So this makes it much cheaper for agents to reuse context, iterate on solutions, and work through longer tasks." According to OpenAI, the model scores higher than Anthropic's Opus 5.5 on GDP.pdf, which measures how accurately models answer professional questions using complex PDF documents, including tables, charts, diagrams, and fine-print details. It also approaches GPT‑6 Astra’s performance on the benchmark at roughly one-fifth the cost per task. On AutomationBench, which measures whether agents correctly complete multi-step business workflows, GPT‑6.1 Sol scores 2.2 percent above Opus 5.5's score at medium reasoning effort, at roughly a third of the cost. On OSWorld 2.0’s offline set, which evaluates agents on demanding computer-use workflows, GPT‑6.1 Sol comes within 2.1 percentage points of Astra’s score at maximum reasoning effort at roughly one-seventh the cost per task. According to OpenAI, GPT‑6.1 Sol also improves factual accuracy on difficult prompts, with the largest factuality improvement over GPT‑6 Sol coming on low reasoning effort, where it reduces the share of responses containing a factual error from 11.4 percent to 7.7 percent, with the overall error rate remaining within 1.9 percentage points of GPT‑6 Astra’s, at less than one-fifth the cost per task. The model's standard API prices are $2 per million input tokens, $0.10 per million cached input tokens, and $10 per million output tokens. And, if you were wondering why OpenAI would launch a new Sol model just a few days after the GPT-6 Sol, it is intended to paper over the embarrassment caused last week. OpenAI's Ultrafast offers up to 8× faster token generation (300 tokens per second) in Codex and up to 6x in the API. Leaked tidbits in recent days had indicated that this tier would be powered by Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine, but OpenAI has yet to confirm it. GPT‑6 Astra Ultrafast is available today in the API⁠ and in ChatGPT Work and Codex⁠ on Pro 500 and Enterprise plans, while GPT‑6.1 Sol Ultrafast is expected to land soon. It costs an insane $60 per 1 million tokens of input and $300 per 1 million tokens of output though! story.title: OpenAI launches Dots, its Muse competitor

facts.text: OpenAI is responding to Meta’s buzzy Muse AI with agentic helpers of its own: Dots.

During its DevDay keynote on Tuesday, OpenAI announced that Dots will serve as always-on AI assistants that can “do nearly anything” across connected apps in the background while learning your preferences over time.
Dots also learn while they work, allowing them to personalize their output and come up with other tasks to complete “before you even think to ask,” according to OpenAI.
OpenAI says Dots come with “built-in rules for when to act independently,” but you can set custom ones that block certain actions or dictate when it should ask for permission.
OpenAI is also testing a feature that lets companies create “specialist” Dots to handle specific roles inside organizations.
The company’s capable GPT-6 Astra model powers Dots, which use their own cloud computer to access a web browser and more than 4,000 supported apps.
It will soon be able to talk to you over text message as well. [Video: OpenAI Dots] For now, you can only create one Dot, though OpenAI plans to allow users to deploy multiple agents at once.
Dots can also connect to Microsoft Teams and Slack, where they will carry over the context from your sessions on other apps and devices.
As an example, OpenAI says a developer working on an app could ask their Dot to use customer feedback to build and test updates, while presenting them with a video showing its changes.
OpenAI notes that conversations with your Dot won’t count toward ChatGPT usage limits.
OpenAI today announced the launch of "Dots" to compete with Meta 's popular Muse agent.
OpenAI describes Dots as always-on agents "built to handle everything."
Dots use the GPT–6 Astra model and have a cloud computer with a web browser, much like Muse.
The agents learn from feedback over time, and OpenAI says they can work on the user's goals "24/7" and connect to over 4,000 apps.
Conversations with the agent don't count toward ChatGPT usage limits, but tasks will use plan allowances.
Dots can be set up in the ChatGPT desktop app and accessed in the mobile app afterward.
Users can communicate with Dots through ChatGPT or other apps like Slack or Teams, and options to text Dots are planned.
Dots follow ChatGPT's permissions and support custom rules for which tasks require approval.
Users can create a "primary dot" and name it starting today, with teams of Dots coming later.
Dots are rolling out for Pro, Business Premium, and Enterprise plans in select markets, with other users to get access soon.

OpenAI introduced Dots at its DevDay 2026 developer conference.
According to the company, they're always-on agents that take over ongoing tasks, keep an eye on projects, and reach out when something needs the user's attention.
Each Dot has its own cloud computer with a browser, so it can work around the clock.
There it does research, analyzes data, writes documents, or builds software through Codex.
Technically, Dots are similar to Meta's Muse agent, which launched three weeks earlier.
OpenAI is going further for businesses with specialized Dots that take on fixed roles inside an organization.
These get their own identity, their own credentials, and, if the company wants, computers supplied by IT.
OpenAI says it has tested them internally in purchasing, invoice processing, email marketing, customer support, and contract management.
The rollout starts with pilot projects at individual companies.
In one internal case, OpenAI says a Dot followed a bug reported in Slack all the way to a working new build.
For an early tester, the agent spotted a forgotten invoice, prepared it, and sent it once the tester approved.
Each user gets one Dot at launch, but OpenAI's long-term plan is whole teams of Dots working together.
Alongside them, OpenAI is releasing GPT-6.1 Sol, a cheaper model.
A Dot can also use saved passwords without the model ever seeing them.
Safeguards are supposed to block malicious instructions, and a monitoring system can pause or stop the work if safety concerns come up.
An Activity View shows what the Dot is working on, including tasks running in the background.
OpenAI admits Dots can make mistakes and recommends double-checking any results that carry real consequences.
Plugins let a Dot connect to more than 4,000 apps and move several projects forward at the same time.
OpenAI says the agent learns from feedback how its user works and what they consider a good result.
Users can reach their Dot through chat or voice calls in ChatGPT, and also in Slack and Microsoft Teams.
The Dot keeps its context across all of these channels, OpenAI says.
OpenAI calls this "proactive research." In this mode, the agent only uses read-only tools, which can't send messages, change content, or control a browser or computer.
For active tasks, a set of ground rules decides when a Dot acts alone and when it checks in first.
Custom Rules let users allow individual actions, require approval for them, or ban them outright.
OpenAI says an automated check reviews any action that touches accounts or shares information against those rules before it goes through.
Sensitive tasks like changing a password always stay with the human.
OpenAI's demos also include everyday errands, like ordering food by text message.
The company says that feature is coming soon.
Users on personal plans decide for themselves whether their Dot's conversations and work can be used for training.
OpenAI also says it doesn't train directly on the background research or the notes a Dot keeps for itself.
For now, Pro subscribers can only use Dots outside the European Economic Area, Switzerland, and the UK.
Business Premium customers get them in all supported regions, while Enterprise, Edu, and Healthcare customers can try a beta once their admins switch it on.
Users set up their Dot in the desktop app or browser first, and after that it's also available on mobile.

Users can communicate with Dots through ChatGPT or other apps like Slack or Teams, and options to text Dots are planned.
Dots follow ChatGPT's permissions and support custom rules for which tasks require approval.
Users can create a "primary dot" and name it starting today, with teams of Dots coming later.
Dots are rolling out for Pro, Business Premium, and Enterprise plans in select markets, with other users to get access soon.
OpenAI introduced Dots at its DevDay 2026 developer conference.
According to the company, they're always-on agents that take over ongoing tasks, keep an eye on projects, and reach out when something needs the user's attention.
Each Dot has its own cloud computer with a browser, so it can work around the clock.
There it does research, analyzes data, writes documents, or builds software through Codex.
Technically, Dots are similar to Meta's Muse agent, which launched three weeks earlier.
OpenAI is going further for businesses with specialized Dots that take on fixed roles inside an organization.
These get their own identity, their own credentials, and, if the company wants, computers supplied by IT.
OpenAI says it has tested them internally in purchasing, invoice processing, email marketing, customer support, and contract management.
The rollout starts with pilot projects at individual companies.
In one internal case, OpenAI says a Dot followed a bug reported in Slack all the way to a working new build.
For an early tester, the agent spotted a forgotten invoice, prepared it, and sent it once the tester approved.
Each user gets one Dot at launch, but OpenAI's long-term plan is whole teams of Dots working together.
Alongside them, OpenAI is releasing GPT-6.1 Sol, a cheaper model.
A Dot can also use saved passwords without the model ever seeing them.
Safeguards are supposed to block malicious instructions, and a monitoring system can pause or stop the work if safety concerns come up.
An Activity View shows what the Dot is working on, including tasks running in the background.
OpenAI admits Dots can make mistakes and recommends double-checking any results that carry real consequences.
Plugins let a Dot connect to more than 4,000 apps and move several projects forward at the same time.
OpenAI says the agent learns from feedback how its user works and what they consider a good result.
Users can reach their Dot through chat or voice calls in ChatGPT, and also in Slack and Microsoft Teams.
The Dot keeps its context across all of these channels, OpenAI says.
OpenAI calls this "proactive research." In this mode, the agent only uses read-only tools, which can't send messages, change content, or control a browser or computer.
For active tasks, a set of ground rules decides when a Dot acts alone and when it checks in first.
Custom Rules let users allow individual actions, require approval for them, or ban them outright.
OpenAI says an automated check reviews any action that touches accounts or shares information against those rules before it goes through.
Sensitive tasks like changing a password always stay with the human.
OpenAI's demos also include everyday errands, like ordering food by text message.
The company says that feature is coming soon.
Users on personal plans decide for themselves whether their Dot's conversations and work can be used for training.
OpenAI also says it doesn't train directly on the background research or the notes a Dot keeps for itself.
For now, Pro subscribers can only use Dots outside the European Economic Area, Switzerland, and the UK.
Business Premium customers get them in all supported regions, while Enterprise, Edu, and Healthcare customers can try a beta once their admins switch it on.
Users set up their Dot in the desktop app or browser first, and after that it's also available on mobile.

OpenAI is finally delivering on the hype that it attempted to build over the past few weeks for its DevDay 2026, replete with over 20 distinct product launches, albeit complicated by an evolving competitive environment where Anthropic has again taken an apparent lead by launching the eminently stellar Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 AI models.
PT, OpenAI will likely unveil personal AI agents called Dots.

In what is a rare bit of positive news, however, Axios has just reported that OpenAI's annual recurring revenue (ARR) is now close to $70 billion ($68 billion to be exact) after growing by over 70 percent since the beginning of Q3 2026.
For reference, Anthropic's ARR hovered near $65 billion in August .
As expected, OpenAI has just unveiled Dots , your personal, always-on AI agents powered by GPT-6 Astra.
With support for OpenAI's plugins, Dots can connect to over 4,000 apps, including ChatGPT, Slack, and Teams.

Also, we can't but help notice that Dots appear to be geared more towards enterprises, which should give Meta's Muse a relatively unhindered path for now to dominate the consumer-oriented personal AI agent space.
The fact that the Dot is only available on the Pro tiers while Meta Muse is free up to a limit will also skew the uptake.
Do note that OpenAI had teased an always-on agent, called "o ," over the weekend.

OpenAI’s new AI agent Dot failed to respond during its first live demo prompting the presenter to say “I guess Dot’s having a slow morning.” I just added to my $META position. pic.twitter.com/dzFDHBYuXA
OpenAI has suffered a series of setbacks recently.

Finally, OpenAI says that Dots are rolling out today in ChatGPT to Pro and Business Premium users in all markets excluding the European Economic Area, Switzerland, and the UK .

WASHINGTON—From the specter of US retrenchment to ongoing Russian revanchism, European NATO members must face up to a harsh reality: the Alliance lacks the industrial capabilities to meet today’s security challenges. Their recent promises to increase defense spending, while substantial and welcome, will not be enough alone to change this. To adapt quickly enough to confront evolving threats, NATO allies must get the basics right. This means adopting functional and flexible financing mechanisms, streamlining regulatory frameworks, and building production foundations that prioritize scalable and sustainable innovation. These challenges that NATO faces, as well as the need for the Alliance to get the basics right, are being actively discussed, including at the 2025 Netherlands-US Defense Industry Days conference in Washington, DC, this past October. At this event, organized by the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands and the Atlantic Council, policymakers, industry leaders, financiers, and experts discussed how transatlantic allies can accelerate defense innovation while strengthening their defense industrial bases. Below are a few of the authors’ major takeaways from this conference on how NATO can meet these challenges. Increasingly, the battlefields of the future will be won in the realm of innovation. Building ecosystems to support technology development will require allies to use newly unlocked defense dollars to fill immediate capability gaps and build flexible financing pathways to foster innovation. If done right, these defense ecosystems can allocate more resources directly to innovators, boosting returns on investment and generating cutting-edge capabilities in North America and Europe. To do this, allies should take a two-pronged approach to financing innovation: Accept risk to accelerate adoption. Many innovation initiatives—such as NATO’s Defense Innovation Accelerator for the North Atlantic (DIANA) organization—too often fall short because they prioritize immediate return on investment or quick-turn results over long-term innovation development. This places a strain on innovators, limiting their access to seed money and signaling to the private sector that the Alliance does not prioritize lasting defense technology innovation. Instead, NATO should give these initiatives greater latitude to prioritize experimentation and iteration rather than meeting often arbitrary metrics and quotas. Protect research and development budgets. From the rise of the space domain to electromagnetic warfare, NATO allies must win not just a single innovation race; they need to win many at once. Research and development (R&D) budgets are critical to this effort. Yet, far too often, as participants at the conference noted, R&D budgets for defense technologies are cannibalized in favor of immediate operational needs, particularly during periods of heightened security pressure. By prioritizing R&D budgets, governments can send a clear signal to defense industries, investment bankers, and venture capitalists that NATO members see investment in defense technology as a long-term and sustainable demand. These signals can help spur greater private-sector investment in these technologies. Current regulatory environments on both sides of the Atlantic are not designed for the speed of innovation or adoption needed in today’s rapidly evolving security environment. Instead, NATO allies must strike a careful balance: NATO countries should impose regulations that protect sensitive technologies and intellectual property while also encouraging cooperation among allies on innovation development. Two main principles should inform this approach: Break down barriers to transatlantic defense industrial cooperation. In the United States, having to navigate dense bureaucracy can stifle innovation, hamper collaborative partnerships, and stretch lead times for critical defense technologies. However, US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth recently made several announcements that show promise in this area—including loosening restrictions on defense contractors and emphasizing speed—indicating that the Pentagon will work to streamline defense cooperation for allies looking to buy US capabilities. Despite this positive momentum, meaningful changes to US foreign military sales and armaments cooperation will require sustained efforts to reform these overly burdensome bureaucratic processes. Keep agile firms top of mind when writing regulations. Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) will make or break the next era of warfare. Yet defense industrial and innovation regulations often impose disproportionate costs on SMEs because they are designed only for the largest defense companies. For example, the US Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification rightly protects sensitive data through third-party audit and monitoring requirements. But as written, the cost of compliance with these regulations is prohibitively expensive for SMEs, risking pushing many smaller defense firms out of the market altogether. Therefore, policymakers and military planners must establish more frequent, institutionalized relationships with SMEs to better understand how regulations affect these new players. A good step in the right direction would be for policymakers to apply regulations on a sliding scale, setting thresholds for how large a defense company must grow before it has to comply with certain requirements. NATO should adopt a holistic approach to capability development that marries research, design, and production to turn industrial development into more than just the sum of its structural parts. Three ways to build this holistic approach are: Champion defense industrial cooperation. To innovate at the necessary pace, the Alliance must build defense industrial co-development, co-production, and co-assembly pathways. Working industry-to-industry or industry-to-partner, such collaborative efforts can help enable allied industries to scale up production and develop cutting-edge defense technologies. This approach defrays risk for industry, builds stronger transatlantic bonds, and shortens lead times for capability delivery. Advance a model that combines expertise across sectors. To build more resilient and sustainable defense innovation ecosystems, allies should foster a defense innovation model that integrates government, industry, and academia. With these three sectors working together, allies can coordinate experimentation, testing, and manufacturing efforts to accelerate development and deployment timelines. Applied across the Atlantic, such a model could replace isolated national pilot projects with a coordinated framework for sustained, interoperable innovation. Establish a NATO Defense Innovation Unit to spur development. Modeled after the United States’ own Defense Innovation Unit, a NATO version of the institution would help the Alliance coordinate funding, regulation, and capability development. A NATO Defense Innovation Unit would maintain shared test facilities, align technical standards, and guide the transition of prototypes into fielded systems. It would serve as a permanent platform connecting NATO’s innovation initiatives—such as DIANA and the NATO Innovation Fund—with national and private-sector efforts. Building transatlantic innovation ecosystems must begin with the basics: financing innovation wisely, regulating for speed and scalability, and building integrated defense innovation models across sectors and allied capitals. A roadmap grounded in smart investment, adaptive regulations, and collaborative production can transform innovation into readiness. These challenges that NATO faces, as well as the need for the Alliance to get the basics right, are being actively discussed, including at the 2025 Netherlands-US Defense Industry Days conference in Washington, DC, this past October. Increasingly, the battlefields of the future will be won in the realm of innovation. If done right, these defense ecosystems can allocate more resources directly to innovators, boosting returns on investment and generating cutting-edge capabilities in North America and Europe.
To do this, allies should take a two-pronged approach to financing innovation:

Accept risk to accelerate adoption. Many innovation initiatives—such as NATO’s Defense Innovation Accelerator for the North Atlantic (DIANA) organization—too often fall short because they prioritize immediate return on investment or quick-turn results over long-term innovation development. This places a strain on innovators, limiting their access to seed money and signaling to the private sector that the Alliance does not prioritize lasting defense technology innovation. Instead, NATO should give these initiatives greater latitude to prioritize experimentation and iteration rather than meeting often arbitrary metrics and quotas.

Protect research and development budgets. From the rise of the space domain to electromagnetic warfare, NATO allies must win not just a single innovation race; they need to win many at once. Research and development (R&D) budgets are critical to this effort. Yet, far too often, as participants at the conference noted, R&D budgets for defense technologies are cannibalized in favor of immediate operational needs, particularly during periods of heightened security pressure. By prioritizing R&D budgets, governments can send a clear signal to defense industries, investment bankers, and venture capitalists that NATO members see investment in defense technology as a long-term and sustainable demand. These signals can help spur greater private-sector investment in these technologies.

Instead, NATO allies must strike a careful balance: NATO countries should impose regulations that protect sensitive technologies and intellectual property while also encouraging cooperation among allies on innovation development. Two main principles should inform this approach:

Break down barriers to transatlantic defense industrial cooperation. In the United States, having to navigate dense bureaucracy can stifle innovation, hamper collaborative partnerships, and stretch lead times for critical defense technologies. However, US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth recently made several announcements that show promise in this area—including loosening restrictions on defense contractors and emphasizing speed—indicating that the Pentagon will work to streamline defense cooperation for allies looking to buy US capabilities. Despite this positive momentum, meaningful changes to US foreign military sales and armaments cooperation will require sustained efforts to reform these overly burdensome bureaucratic processes.

Keep agile firms top of mind when writing regulations. Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) will make or break the next era of warfare. Yet defense industrial and innovation regulations often impose disproportionate costs on SMEs because they are designed only for the largest defense companies. For example, the US Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification rightly protects sensitive data through third-party audit and monitoring requirements. But as written, the cost of compliance with these regulations is prohibitively expensive for SMEs, risking pushing many smaller defense firms out of the market altogether. Therefore, policymakers and military planners must establish more frequent, institutionalized relationships with SMEs to better understand how regulations affect these new players. A good step in the right direction would be for policymakers to apply regulations on a sliding scale, setting thresholds for how large a defense company must grow before it has to comply with certain requirements.

NATO should adopt a holistic approach to capability development that marries research, design, and production to turn industrial development into more than just the sum of its structural parts. Three ways to build this holistic approach are:

Champion defense industrial cooperation. To innovate at the necessary pace, the Alliance must build defense industrial co-development, co-production, and co-assembly pathways. Working industry-to-industry or industry-to-partner, such collaborative efforts can help enable allied industries to scale up production and develop cutting-edge defense technologies. This approach defrays risk for industry, builds stronger transatlantic bonds, and shortens lead times for capability delivery.

Advance a model that combines expertise across sectors. To build more resilient and sustainable defense innovation ecosystems, allies should foster a defense innovation model that integrates government, industry, and academia. With these three sectors working together, allies can coordinate experimentation, testing, and manufacturing efforts to accelerate development and deployment timelines. Applied across the Atlantic, such a model could replace isolated national pilot projects with a coordinated framework for sustained, interoperable innovation.

Establish a NATO Defense Innovation Unit to spur development. Modeled after the United States’ own Defense Innovation Unit, a NATO version of the institution would help the Alliance coordinate funding, regulation, and capability development. A NATO Defense Innovation Unit would maintain shared test facilities, align technical standards, and guide the transition of prototypes into fielded systems. It would serve as a permanent platform connecting NATO’s innovation initiatives—such as DIANA and the NATO Innovation Fund—with national and private-sector efforts.

Building transatlantic innovation ecosystems must begin with the basics: financing innovation wisely, regulating for speed and scalability, and building integrated defense innovation models across sectors and allied capitals. A roadmap grounded in smart investment, adaptive regulations, and collaborative production can transform innovation into readiness.

sources.title: Biden’s Plans for NATO Strategically Reimagine the Transatlantic Relationship - Georgetown Security Studies Review
passages: For all of this to be possible, however, NATO needs to be step up its political game.

Biden’s plans to “elevate diplomacy as the United States’ principal tool of foreign policy” will be essential for an organization that requires consensus across 30 disparate nations to move. [viii] Vice President Biden also has a long journey ahead to reassure European allies of America’s resolve to lead, particularly when American citizens’ investment in European security has soured in recent years.
One such gesture to start the healing process would be the Summit for Democracy he intends to convene in the first year of his administration.

By bringing together the world’s democracies on an equal footing early in his first term, Vice President Biden aims to unite around a common agenda not only with allied nations, but also with civil society organizations, technology companies, and non-governmental organizations.

Together, this coalition will align threat assessments and develop cohesive strategies to tackle them as one. [ix] NATO should hold a prominent seat at this summit’s table in addition to individual national representation.
NATO members recommitting to their democratic responsibilities offers a sort of vow renewal for the transatlantic marriage that will be key moving forward.

With the 2020 US presidential election, it’s important to remember that Americans have not only elected the President of the United States, but also the leader of the free world responsible for reuniting the divided transatlantic community.
Mastering this equilibrium starts with reaffirming NATO’s value amongst an American populace that has frequently heard arguments that the alliance is no longer valuable.

Biden jokingly claims that NATO and finding a cure for cancer are the only two things Democrats and Republicans agree upon, but he may be right. [v] To unite the country and the transatlantic community, Biden views NATO as the proper vehicle to ensure collective security while reinforcing shared identities and interests.
In fact, Biden’s argument at the Munich Security Conference last year emphasized this fact to a shared North Atlantic audience.

He tried to assuage Europeans’ fears that they would be abandoned by an “America First” US by claiming, “You can count on us to lead…because it is overwhelmingly in our self-interest” and that of other countries’.
Starting straight at the camera, he promised: “We will be back.” [vi] It seems NATO trusts this commitment as well.

In a surprisingly partisan move for the Alliance, it announced that it would welcome a President Biden to Brussels for a summit in early spring, whereas a summit with a reelected President Trump would wait until the summer. [vii] This shift makes sense in terms of the policy agenda both candidates would seek to assert, as Trump would likely have fewer and far more divisive initiatives than Biden would.
Regardless, the move speaks volumes for an alliance that values American membership dearly.
When it comes to China, again Biden’s policy tilts toward alliances as a tool to both project and enhance American power.

That is a substantial segment of the international economy for China to contend with, especially when it needs Western markets and cooperation to work on labor, trade, and technology issues. [xviii] Here NATO could serve as an effective model for America’s hub-and-spoke network of alliances and relations with Indo-Pacific partners.

Working as one transpacific community, united with the transatlantic community at our back, NATO and its East and South Asian partners could address the security threats China poses. [xix] As a political alliance, NATO can provide a forum for robust diplomatic discussions and lend security sector reform expertise to Indo-Pacific allies facing an encroaching Chinese influence.
President-elect Biden is the sum of his 47 years of political office.

Whether facing off against climate change, China, or Covid, Biden’s strategies all incorporate allies. NATO is uniquely placed among the United States’ many bilateral and multilateral alliances to be at the forefront of this strategy. Critical to overturning some Americans’ negative view of NATO, however, will be the issue of burden-sharing. President Trump decimated transatlantic solidarity over the critical 2% of GDP spending requirements on defense issues—a pledge actually negotiated by the Obama Administration. [iii] The commitment divided allies, particularly when resources for coronavirus are eating a larger share of federal budgets. Ironically, however, Trump’s push for European allies to step up may increase the bargaining space for a Biden administration. Biden acknowledges the challenges emanating from Russian electoral interference, the erosion of democratic institutions across NATO member-states, and the threats of disruptive technology and 5G wielded by a revisionist China. As a result, the Biden administration would likely revise and expand its definition of burden-sharing. Far from a largely symbolic 2% pledge, Biden has an opportunity to push for burden-sharing in terms of capabilities, with principles ordered to exact change, enhance defense and deterrence posture, and ensure the Alliance is fit for a new geopolitical era. [iv] Mastering this equilibrium starts with reaffirming NATO’s value amongst an American populace that has frequently heard arguments that the alliance is no longer valuable. Biden jokingly claims that NATO and finding a cure for cancer are the only two things Democrats and Republicans agree upon, but he may be right. [v] To unite the country and the transatlantic community, Biden views NATO as the proper vehicle to ensure collective security while reinforcing shared identities and interests. In fact, Biden’s argument at the Munich Security Conference last year emphasized this fact to a shared North Atlantic audience. [x] When it comes to technology, Biden has proposed that a U.S.-led coalition of countries should develop shared norms for cyberspace. [xxi] Biden’s foreign policy aims to make America “a light to the world once again.” [xxii] The Biden Administration can wield a real strategic advantage in executing its ambitious foreign policy agenda and ensuring a transatlantic community free, whole, and at peace. relevantPassages.text: For all of this to be possible, however, NATO needs to be step up its political game.

Biden’s plans to “elevate diplomacy as the United States’ principal tool of foreign policy” will be essential for an organization that requires consensus across 30 disparate nations to move. [viii] Vice President Biden also has a long journey ahead to reassure European allies of America’s resolve to lead, particularly when American citizens’ investment in European security has soured in recent years.
One such gesture to start the healing process would be the Summit for Democracy he intends to convene in the first year of his administration.

By bringing together the world’s democracies on an equal footing early in his first term, Vice President Biden aims to unite around a common agenda not only with allied nations, but also with civil society organizations, technology companies, and non-governmental organizations.

Together, this coalition will align threat assessments and develop cohesive strategies to tackle them as one. [ix] NATO should hold a prominent seat at this summit’s table in addition to individual national representation.
NATO members recommitting to their democratic responsibilities offers a sort of vow renewal for the transatlantic marriage that will be key moving forward.

With the 2020 US presidential election, it’s important to remember that Americans have not only elected the President of the United States, but also the leader of the free world responsible for reuniting the divided transatlantic community.
Mastering this equilibrium starts with reaffirming NATO’s value amongst an American populace that has frequently heard arguments that the alliance is no longer valuable.

Biden jokingly claims that NATO and finding a cure for cancer are the only two things Democrats and Republicans agree upon, but he may be right. [v] To unite the country and the transatlantic community, Biden views NATO as the proper vehicle to ensure collective security while reinforcing shared identities and interests.
In fact, Biden’s argument at the Munich Security Conference last year emphasized this fact to a shared North Atlantic audience.

He tried to assuage Europeans’ fears that they would be abandoned by an “America First” US by claiming, “You can count on us to lead…because it is overwhelmingly in our self-interest” and that of other countries’.
Starting straight at the camera, he promised: “We will be back.” [vi] It seems NATO trusts this commitment as well.

In a surprisingly partisan move for the Alliance, it announced that it would welcome a President Biden to Brussels for a summit in early spring, whereas a summit with a reelected President Trump would wait until the summer. [vii] This shift makes sense in terms of the policy agenda both candidates would seek to assert, as Trump would likely have fewer and far more divisive initiatives than Biden would.
Regardless, the move speaks volumes for an alliance that values American membership dearly.
When it comes to China, again Biden’s policy tilts toward alliances as a tool to both project and enhance American power.

That is a substantial segment of the international economy for China to contend with, especially when it needs Western markets and cooperation to work on labor, trade, and technology issues. [xviii] Here NATO could serve as an effective model for America’s hub-and-spoke network of alliances and relations with Indo-Pacific partners.

Working as one transpacific community, united with the transatlantic community at our back, NATO and its East and South Asian partners could address the security threats China poses. [xix] As a political alliance, NATO can provide a forum for robust diplomatic discussions and lend security sector reform expertise to Indo-Pacific allies facing an encroaching Chinese influence.
President-elect Biden is the sum of his 47 years of political office.
The father of an Iraq War veteran, he chaired the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and negotiated with allies worldwide as vice-president under the Obama administration.
Central to his foreign policy are relationships.
Joe Biden places alliances at the center of any foreign policy initiative he envisions to protect the international order, safeguard American democracy, and advance peace and prosperity worldwide.
Whether facing off against climate change, China, or Covid, Biden’s strategies all incorporate allies.

Biden’s approach to Russia boils down to three objectives: “pursue deterrence, cooperation, and strategic stability with Moscow;” jointly impose costs on Russia with our allies; and sustain the pressure until the Minsk agreements are implemented. [xiii] NATO can be useful to Washington’s Russia strategy if it takes steps towards Georgian and Ukrainian membership, enhancement of energy security, and prevention and attribution of cyberattacks.
